If you’ve been forwarded this Playbook, you can sign up free to get it each weekday morning.

ESSENTIALS

— KPMG raking it in, despite ban on new work

— Surprise compliments for Chris Bowen

— One Nation and Liberal paths to power in Victoria

DRIVING THE DAY

KPMG’s $38.5 MILLION TRICKLE

Imagine you lose most of a massive federal government funding stream and you’re forced to make do with just $38.5M in new additional income over 3 months. That’s life at KPMG this quarter.

Yes: Tens of millions for contracts and amendments have flowed to KPMG — from six departments — while the firm has been banned from bidding for new federal government work.

Miriam Webber used Tendertrace and AusTender to analyze the $38.5 million of contracts and amendments. The Department of Defence shoveled nearly $30 million to KPMG.

Some of the deals were executed before the Jun. 16 ban but didn’t kick in until afterwards, the rest were amendments to existing contracts. These are all allowed under the terms of the ban and Finance says it isn’t aware of anyone breaking the rules.

It shows just how much the federal government currently relies on KPMG. The government has until Oct. 31 to figure out how to deal with procurement going forward.

A similar thing happened with PwC Australia, which was banned from federal government work for more than a year.

Yes, but: It had already sold off its government advisory business — which became Scyne Advisory, and was able to quickly take up at least some of the space left by PwC.

The Department of Finance in June told agencies to stop awarding work to the firm from June 16 to Sept. 30 — later extended until Oct. 31. Finance asked former senior public servant Ian Watt to investigate KPMG’s ethical soundness, after whistleblower allegations that it used confidential client information to win work.

Read Miriam’s full article.

SAVING(S) THE DAY: Treasurer Jim Chalmers told “Insiders” on Sunday that he’s working on a savings package to be unveiled in his Mid-Year Economic and Fiscal Outlook in December.

The tease comes as voters start to think more and more about economic management, which jumped seven percentage points as an issue of concern in the AFR’s latest RedBridge Group/Accent Research poll.

The cost of living is the number one issue of concern in the poll. Economic management has still not made the top five. In the same interview, Chalmers put the emphasis on savings — skirting around a question on extra cost-of-living relief by saying people will expect a “tight ship.”

THE PLAYBOOK INTERVIEW

EU COMMISSIONER WOPKE HOEKSTRA — “CHRIS BOWEN HAS DONE AN ABSOLUTELY INCREDIBLE JOB”

Hoekstra is flying above the Pacific as you read this, en route to Fiji for a major pre-COP negotiations summit, largely funded by Australia. Hoekstra serves as the European commissioner for climate, net zero and clean growth, representing the 27 EU governments in Fiji discussions (though some will send their own ministers). He spoke to Playbook’s Ryan Heath via video call over the weekend.

This transcript has been edited for length and clarity. 

Pacific nation leaders see climate action is a matter of survival. This year’s COP is very much about practical action. What is Europe committing to? 

For our friends and partners from the islands, both the Pacific and the Caribbean, one meter [of sea rise] is wet feet. Two meters means I need to move uphill. Three meters is drowning.

The essence of this COP is the whole topic of electrification: practical, high impact, and relatively non-controversial. If we, as a global community, manage to double down on solar, on on wind, on battery capacity, on grid investments, on nuclear, that is really going to be a game changer.

[Climate and Energy Minister Chris] Bowen is accused of not mobilizing enough leaders. How are you feeling about the seniority in Fiji? 

If my cheat sheet is correct, European ministers’ participation at the pre-COP is higher than at UNGA [in New York], and I negotiate at the core on behalf of the EU 27. We are showing how committed we are to our exceptionally close partners in Australia and the Pacific.

Chris Bowen has done an absolutely incredible job in terms of proactive outreach, shaping the conversations, building bridges. I have been active in international politics for close to a decade as a finance minister, as a foreign minister, and as a [European] commissioner. So it’s grounded in experience when I’m saying that he is really doing a very, very good job in a hugely complicated geopolitical environment.

We’re deep into the energy transition: a massive solar transition, EVs lead the car sales now. How does that progress effect the politics of pushing forward? Does it make it inevitable?

It is clearly inevitable from a climate perspective, and from the perspective of competitiveness and independence.

Europe is importing more than 80% of its gas and more than 95% of its oil. That is a phenomenally large political liability. Those in Europe who have been at the forefront of electrification can now provide their citizens with far lower energy prices because they are far less dependent on oil and gas.

This transition is accepted across the political spectrum in places like Finland and Denmark, because it is cheaper, and the business community is actually asking for more of it.

You can always have a debate that needs to be fact-based on how to make sure you do this transition in the most cost-effective way. You need to be in the mindset to never be dogmatic and to always learn.

For all the discussions around a sovereign Europe — security, artificial intelligence, etc. — the sovereignty is actually coming in more practical forms through the energy transition.

Exactly, exactly. In the Benelux [Belgium, Netherlands, Luxembourg] and northern countries, the penetration rate of newly sold electric vehicles is far higher than 50%.

The Finnish — and they did it because they wanted to never ever have a dependency on Russia — have doubled down on renewables and on nuclear and have the best grid network maybe in the world. They have energy abundance. They have the lowest prices across Europe.

THE RESILIENCE MAP BEHIND ONE NATION’S RISE 

Australia’s capacity to absorb a shock is uneven, and that makes it harder for politicians to manage voter frustrations, according to a new effort to map Australian financial, social and health resilience (as distinct from security and emergency-based resilience).

“A single disadvantage score would put Cessnock and Cabramatta in the same bucket. The index does not and that is a critical distinction,” said RedBridge’s Kos Samaras.

Australia’s first neighborhood-level resilience index, based on research, by Zurich, Mandala and RedBridge and Accent Research, found that:

— Regional communities are most exposed on health.

— Many outer and middle suburban communities are more exposed on finances and social connection.

— Adelaide’s north and parts of outer Brisbane face pressure across all three pillars.

STARK PATTERNS

— Nearly 4 million Australians aged 15 to 69 live in communities rated as having low or very low resilience, with roughly the same number having high or very high resilience.

— The national average conceals exceptional gaps: Community scores range from 12.3 in East Arnhem to 78.9 in Cottesloe. The ACT average is highest, at 52.0, more than 8 points above the national average of 43.5. The report says no ACT community is rated low or very low.

— Regional health is the sharpest national divide: Roughly 2 in 3 regional Australians lack health resilience, compared to 1 in 10 in major cities.

— The politics of belonging: 46% of people feel like a stranger in their own country. The measure peaks at 61% in Lingiari, home to large indigenous communities.

— Housing stress cuts across the resilience map: 1 in 3 Australians is in housing stress, no matter how rich your neighborhood. High resilience communities cope with it better, naturally.

— Some places face strain across the board. Spence, in Adelaide’s outer northern suburbs, is the report’s lowest-scoring electorate, and its hub Elizabeth, 27% are reported to lack access to emergency funds, 38% of adults smoke and 18% report a mental health condition.

— Gender gap concentrated in midlife. Women score 41.3 nationally, compared with 45.7 for men. Women aged 35 to 49 are the lowest-scoring group at 40.3; 1 in 3 is in a low or very low resilience community, compared with 1 in 8 men of the same age.

— Tasmania devil in the details: Tasmania has the weakest health resilience score, while its social resilience is the strongest of any state.

POLITICO TAKEAWAYS FOR UPCOMING ELECTIONS

— One Nation’s path to power is now wider: One Nation has multiple political openings — it’s no longer confined to playing a race card or reaching out to those feeling left behind by globalization.

— Singular cost-of-living messages will probably fail: Parties will need to show they understand the specific local pressure voters are reacting to.

— Who is most exposed to an anti-incumbent swing? In cities, its MPs in outer Brisbane, including Blair, Longman and Forde, and Adelaide’s north. In regional Australia, it’s every MP.

As One Nation vowed to jail former Premiers Jacinta Allan and Dan Andrews and federal opposition frontbencher Tim Wilson branded Labor “an organised crime cartel.” ABC’s chief elections and data analyst Casey Briggs maps out the Liberals’ path to power.

Jess Wilson will find it nearly impossible to become premier without One Nation support, including because nine Nationals seats are at risk of One Nation takeover. But the prospect of handing victory to Labor seems unappealing to three-quarters of voters (they’ve been in power 33 of the past 44 years).

QUEENSLAND DATA CENTER HYPOCRISY ALERT: The QLD government, which insisted on flexibility for itself at National Cabinet on how to power data centers, is refusing to give local councils any flexibility on approving proposed facilities. The Queensland government will take the planning and assessment of data center applications away from local councils under a new system, ABC reported.

ABOUT THAT CREDIT CARD SURCHARGE BAN: It’s become a wildly mishandled policy change — a supposed win for consumers that has mostly left small businesses furious and many consumers paying more for their coffee. (Was Playbook the only one facing weird prices on the weekend? Ryan’s iced flat white was suddenly $6.51, a transaction fee added to the bill.)

Playbook asked the ACCC for its views on the policy change, to be directed back to its August 2025 submission to the RBA.

The TL;DR: ACCC broadly supported the RBA’s package, including because the old system left debit card users subsidizing the higher costs and loyalty rewards programs of high-end credit cards.

Crucially, the ACCC wanted the government to legislate a surcharge ban with a transition period included — and neither happened.

What’s happening? Elections NZ is running an ASMR enrollment ad. The enrollment deadline is Oct. 25.

No word yet on whether it will be a closed grants program or a competitive process.

PARTY ROOM

THE GREENS — MAX EXPOSURE

Former federal MP Max Chandler-Mather has been circulating an open letter calling for the federal Greens to ensure the next vote for leader is cast by the members of the party. He made the call ahead of the Greens party-room vote that saw David Shoebridge elected as leader.

“We say we want to build a movement. That we want to take on billionaires and big corporations,” his letter dated Sept. 29 reads. “But if we’re serious about that it means putting real power and trust in the hands of ordinary people – and trusting they will make the right choice.”

He’s gaining some traction — state members including WA’s Sophie McNeill, Kobi Shetty in NSW and Aiv Puglielli from Victoria — have added their names to a copy seen by Playbook.

LIBERAL — LOUISE CLEGG UNFILTERED: The Spectator columnist and political spouse opened up over an hour with Peter Lewis and Damian Damjanovski in their “What’s Your Poison” podcast.

Clegg covers a lot of ground, from her “Joh for PM” father to her husband Angus Taylor and her professional love for “awesome” High Court Chief Justice Stephen Gageler, a Labor appointee. She also covers why she sees ICAC is a kangaroo court, her views on the U.K. is a legal “basket case,” and why she’s still open to an Indigenous constitutional amendment.

On Taylor: “He’s very nerdy. … He’s not dancing on the table. … He would do better if he was more narcissistic.”

HOW A FAILED ATTACK IN GERMANY REVEALED RUSSIA’S CAMPAIGN HAND: On Aug. 4, a drone struck the wing of a Ukrainian aircraft at Germany’s Leipzig Airport and fell onto the tarmac. Strapped beneath it was a tin can packed with explosives. The device remained intact.

That gave investigators something unusually valuable: the bomb itself. The can was sealed with a metal plate stamped with seven circular indentations, according to an investigative file from German federal police reviewed by the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network.

]]> en Former Belgian PM Verhofstadt investigated in EU Parliament intern probe https://www.politico.eu/article/former-belgium-prime-minister-guy-verhofstadt-european-parliament-intern-probe/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Sun, 04 Oct 2026 17:46:27 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9102896 BRUSSELS — Former Belgian Prime Minister Guy Verhofstadt is under investigation by Belgian federal prosecutors over the supervision of European Parliament interns during his time as leader of the liberal group.

The investigation, which was first reported by Belgian magazine Knack, apparently began this year. It focuses on the period from 2009  to 2019 when Verhofstadt chaired the Alliance of Liberals and Democrats for Europe group in the Parliament. ALDE was succeeded by Renew Europe after the 2019 European election.

An EU official familiar with the matter, who was granted anonymity to speak freely, confirmed to POLITICO that Verhofstadt is under investigation for the way in which he supervised parliamentary interns. They said the probe was initiated by the European Anti-Fraud Office (OLAF) and the European Public Prosecutor’s Office (EPPO), but is now being conducted by Belgian authorities on behalf of the EU bodies.

“OLAF has merely requested information from our client regarding the supervision of a number of interns … in which he, as group chair, was not personally involved,” lawyers Christine Mussche and Quinten De Keersmaecker, who are representing Verhofstadt in the case, told Knack.

“Verhofstadt himself has not yet been interviewed, and there are currently no specific allegations against him. He is cooperating fully with OLAF and has provided the requested explanations with complete transparency,” the lawyers added.

Reached by POLITICO, Verhofstadt declined to comment further.

In a written reply Sunday, EPPO spokesperson Tine Hollevoet said: “As a general rule, the EPPO does not comment on ongoing investigations, nor do we publicly confirm which cases we are working on, in order not to endanger the possible ongoing procedures and their outcome.”

The Belgian Federal Prosecutor’s Office did not immediately respond to a request for comment. 

Verhofstadt, who was Belgium’s prime minister from 1999 to 2008 and served as an MEP from 2009 to 2024, is a prominent pro-EU figure who represented the European Parliament in the Brexit negotiations following the U.K.’s 2016 referendum on EU membership.

He left the Parliament in 2024 and is currently president of the board of the European Movement International, a pro-Europe lobby.

]]> en Le calendrier chargé d’Emmanuel Macron complique sa venue à la COP31 https://www.politico.eu/article/le-calendrier-charge-demmanuel-macron-complique-sa-venue-a-la-cop31/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Sun, 04 Oct 2026 16:35:13 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro&p=9098510 PARIS — Ira ou n’ira pas ? Emmanuel Macron laisse planer le doute sur sa participation à la COP31 — la dernière de son double mandat —, qui aura lieu à Antalya, en Turquie.

Ce pourrait être mal engagé : prévu les 11 et 12 novembre, le sommet des dirigeants de la COP31, qui rassemble traditionnellement les chefs d’Etat et de gouvernement, se chevauche avec les commémorations de la fin de la Première Guerre mondiale et le Forum de Paris sur la paix. Ce conflit d’agenda complique la venue du président français, indiquent à POLITICO deux conseillers de l’exécutif.

La possibilité d’un déplacement en Turquie, pays hôte, le 12 novembre — et donc d’un passage express à la COP — n’est toutefois pas complètement exclue à ce stade. “Si ça se trouve, il a déjà décidé qu’il y allait”, tempère ainsi l’un des conseillers mentionnés plus haut.

Reste que pour le moment, l’intérêt d’Emmanuel Macron pour le grand raout des discussions climatiques demeure timide : invité à prendre part à la pré-COP, qui se tiendra du lundi 3 au jeudi 8 octobre aux Fidji, il a laissé la priorité à sa ministre de la Transition écologique, Monique Barbut.

De “Make our planet great again” au détricotage

Cette attitude tranche avec les débuts au pouvoir de celui qui se plaçait alors en héritier de l’Accord de Paris, dont l’objectif est de contenir le réchauffement climatique “bien en dessous” de 2 °C. A peine un mois après son élection, en juin 2017, le président de la République avait ainsi trouvé un écho international en prononçant le discours “Make our planet great again”, en réponse à Donald Trump qui venait d’annoncer le (premier) retrait des Etats-Unis du traité.

Dix ans plus tard, les avancées écologiques du premier quinquennat ont pour partie été détricotées lors du second, sur la rénovation thermique des bâtiments ou la lutte contre l’artificialisation des sols, entre autres. Ces reculs ont eu des conséquences sur l’influence de la France sur la scène internationale, analysait auprès de POLITICO, en juin 2025, Arnaud Gilles, ancien porte-parole du WWF et spécialiste des questions environnementales.

Le risque d’une image ternie à l’international

Ce n’est pas la première fois qu’Emmanuel Macron laisse planer le doute sur sa venue au sommet mondial sur le climat. L’an dernier, il avait officialisé son intention de s’y rendre un peu plus d’une semaine avant l’événement. Il n’était finalement resté que quelques heures sur place, à Belém, le temps d’une escale entre deux visites d’Etat au Brésil et au Mexique. Il s’était également montré discret lors des célébrations du 10e anniversaire des Accords de Paris.

Une impasse sur le dernier sommet mondial sur le climat de son mandat viendrait écorner un peu plus l’image de champion de l’écologie qu’Emmanuel Macron cherche à renvoyer à l’international. D’autres n’ont pas traîné pour officialiser leur participation. Le Premier ministre britannique, le travailliste Andy Burnham, l’a annoncée dès sa première allocution parlementaire, début septembre, après son accession au pouvoir.

With almost all votes counted following Saturday’s election, the center-right United List won around 35% of the vote — more than 20 percentage points ahead of the far-right Latvia First party, led by veteran politician Ainārs Šlesers, who opposes restrictive tariffs on Russia.

Preliminary results released on Sunday put United List on course for 42 of the 100 seats in the national parliament.

Despite the decisive victory — far stronger than pre-election polling suggested — Kulbergs will still need to negotiate with other parties to form a majority government.

Two partners in his outgoing coalition, the conservative National Alliance and center-right New Unity, cleared the 5% threshold and are set to return to parliament. They appear to have enough seats for a majority without the Union of Greens and Farmers, which fell below the threshold.

That gives Kulbergs a solid path to another pro-Ukraine coalition without having to seek support from Šlesers’ Latvia First, an option that had loomed over the election campaign, which was marked by high inflation, uncertainty around the troubled national airline airBaltic and instrumentalized migration orchestrated by Russia and Belarus.

Kulbergs became prime minister in late May after his predecessor, Evika Siliņa, stood down following a backlash over stray Ukrainian drone strikes. 

The final stretch of Latvia’s election campaign also spilled into Brussels last week, where Kulbergs initially opposed an EU deal to remove Russian billionaires Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman from the bloc’s sanctions list.

Latvia ultimately abstained, allowing the broader sanctions regime to be extended after a compromise among EU countries.

Mehr als die Hälfte der jungen Wähler entscheidet sich bei jüngsten Landtagswahlen für Parteien, die der Ukraine-Unterstützung kritisch gegenüberstehen. Der Grund dafür liegt nicht nur in klassischen Debatten, sondern auf Plattformen wie TikTok, Instagram und X. Dort tobt längst ein massiver Informationskrieg, in dem ausländische Akteure und Algorithmen um die Deutungshoheit kämpfen.

Marcel Bohnert, Oberstleutnant des Heeres der Bundeswehr, kennt diese hybride Kriegsführung aus nächster Nähe. Er analysiert, wie gezielte Desinformationskampagnen, Bot-Netzwerke und gefälschte Nachrichtenseiten die öffentliche Meinung in Deutschland manipulieren. Dabei wird deutlich, warum nicht-militärische Mittel in diesem Konflikt längst eine weitaus größere Rolle spielen als klassische Waffen.

Im Gespräch mit Rixa Fürsen geht es um die drängende Frage, wie sich Demokratien im digitalen Raum überhaupt noch wehren können. Die Folge liefert tiefe Einblicke in die Mechanismen der Propaganda und zeigt auf, welche Strategien im Netz helfen, um die Wahrheit gegen eine Übermacht aus Fake News zu verteidigen.

In contrast to previous visits from Western leaders, during which Moscow had largely refrained from attacks on the Ukrainian capital, air raid sirens could be heard in Kyiv during Merz’s visit. Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko reported that Russia had struck the roadway of the North Bridge in the city. On Saturday, Russia’s foreign ministry issued a warning against foreign visitors and diplomats and urged them to leave Kyiv.

This is Merz’s first bilateral visit to Kyiv and his second trip as chancellor, after travelling there in May 2025 visit alongside leaders from France, the U.K. and Poland.

“If we fail to stop Moscow, sooner or later the Russian war machine will turn against us”, Merz said upon arrival in the Ukrainian capital, adding: “I will tell President Zelenskyy today, ‘You can continue to count on our help.’”

It comes just a few days after the embattled chancellor vowed to maintain his government’s strong support to Ukraine, despite the rise of the far-right, Russia-friendly Alternative für Deutschland (AfD).

During a speech in Münster, Germany, Merz warned that, “in a few weeks, the fifth winter of the war will begin”, which “likely be the hardest one yet.”

Ukrainians “are bracing themselves for intense ballistic missile attacks, for destroyed power plants and schools, and for damaged apartment buildings and churches. Ukraine must survive this winter, and I am convinced that it will. It can count on our help,” Merz added, highlighting German help such as new interception systems against jet drones or repairs for bombed power plants.

Merz and Zelenskyy held a call on Wednesday, which focused on convincing European and international allies like Japan to deliver more Patriot air defense missiles to Ukraine as well as procuring fresh ammunition for Kyiv’s F-16 fighter jets, which are efficient in downing Russian jet drones with their onboard cannon.

Last month, German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius announced that Germany would transfer Patriot PAC-2 interceptor missiles from its own stocks to Ukraine, and called on other states to follow suit.

Following the attempted drone attack on a Ukrainian cargo plane in Leipzig in August, for which Germany blamed Russia, Berlin announced that its intelligence services would help Ukraine with supplying targeting data for long-distance strikes against Russia’s military as well as its industrial base.

Merz has refused to supply Germany’s prized Taurus cruise missiles to Ukraine, despite calling for it when he was opposition leader. Yet his government delivered financial and technical assistance for the development of Ukraine’s own long-range weapons. On Thursday, Zelenskyy announced the successful test of Ukraine’s FP-7 ballistic tactical missile.

German Economy Minister Katherina Reiche, from Merz’s center-right CDU party, joined the trip alongside representatives from a dozen German energy, chemical and drone manufacturing companies, which will participate in a German-Ukrainian economic forum in Kyiv on Sunday.

There are tensions between Merz and Zelenskyy when it comes to Ukraine’s desire to swiftly join the European Union.

The German Chancellor has voiced skepticism that an EU accession would be possible in the coming years and instead proposed an “associated membership” that would grant Ukraine access to the EU’s single market and an observer status in the Council of the EU, the European Commission and the European Parliament, but without any voting rights.

Zelenskyy, however, has rejected the proposal, saying that Ukraine needs “full and equal” membership.

Merz’s visit comes amid renewed attempts to seek a peace agreement between Russia and Ukraine. German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul, who met with his Russia counterpart Sergei Lavrov in New York last weekend, has welcomed a U.S. invite for Vladimir Putin to the G20 leaders’ summit in Miami in December, saying it could be a chance for serious negotiations.

However, so far “Russia’s leadership shows no real interest in putting an end to its deeply inhumane fantasies of subjugation and conquest,” Wadephul said on Friday. “It intends to continue the war against Ukraine.”

]]> en EU neighbors shun Kyiv’s plea to free trapped grain https://www.politico.eu/article/eu-neighbors-shun-kyivs-plea-to-free-trapped-grain/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Sun, 04 Oct 2026 05:00:00 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro&p=9099842 BRUSSELS — Domestic farmers’ worries are trumping EU solidarity with Kyiv as the Black Sea blockade threatens to fuel a global food crisis and stunt Ukraine’s next harvest.

Ukraine needs help getting millions of tons of grain exports out of the country, as attacks on ports and ships continue into a third month.

Agriculture Minister Taras Vysotskyi came to Brussels this week to make a direct appeal to his EU counterparts. Ukraine needs to be able to move more farm products through Europe, as well as €1.1 billion to cover higher shipping costs. Without help, cash-strapped farmers won’t be able to start planting for next season, compounding the problem.

“It’s very, very critical,” Vysotskyi told POLITICO during his visit.

The answer: Sorry, but no. Two of the countries with the most vital infrastructure for boosting shipping and storage capacity, Poland and Romania, said there is nothing more they can or will do to help.

“The interest for our own farmers remains a priority,” Barna Tánczos, Romania’s agriculture minister, told POLITICO. Excess Ukrainian grain, combined with low water levels on the Danube, is already overloading his country’s ports, preventing Romanian farmers from selling their own goods.

The rebuff illustrates a persistent gap between the EU’s ambitions to support Ukraine and domestic political realities. As one of the world’s breadbaskets, Ukraine poses a real threat to the livelihoods of European farmers, a powerful constituency in many member countries. Even before the latest eruption in Black Sea fighting, Poland, Slovakia and Hungary barred imports of Ukrainian grain.

Currently, less than half of the exports are able to get out through the European rail, road and river shipping routes, Vysotskyi said. Up to 35 million tons could end up being stuck in Ukraine this year if the blockade persists.

Romania is trying to optimize its logistics, Tánczos stressed. Last month, Bucharest even signed a memorandum of understanding to ease border crossings with Kyiv and boost rail links.

But “everybody knows we cannot double the number of trains, we cannot double the roads, railways and port capacity,” Tánczos said. “It is what it is.”

In Poland, the infrastructure ministry “has no plans to introduce any changes aimed at increasing the transit of Ukrainian agricultural products,” spokesperson Anna Szumańska said in a statement.

Though help isn’t coming immediately, the EU isn’t ruling out a collective response. “We need … to address this,” Agriculture Commissioner Christophe Hansen told reporters this week, citing concerns for global food security — though he made no commitments.

Some capitals are volunteering more support. As Ukraine eyes Dutch and German ports as new outlets, a German agriculture ministry spokesperson said Berlin “is making every effort in Europe to ensure that alternative export routes … are strengthened.”

Spiraling to next season

In an interview, Vysotskyi described harvested grain and oilseeds piling up without a buyer — leaving farmers without the cash they need to plant winter seeds now for next year’s harvest. “If the situation stays like this till spring, it could mean the decrease of even 35-40% of the planted area,” he said.

The pain will be felt beyond Europe. As Russia and Ukraine trade bombs in the Black Sea, more than 17 percent of the world’s traded grain could be affected by the drop in exports from both countries, according to a recent Council on Foreign Relations report. “The number of people driven into acute hunger by the current Black Sea crisis could exceed all recorded battlefield casualties in the Russia-Ukraine war,” the report warns.

Yet the pain for European farmers — struggling with drought, heatwaves and spiking prices for fuel and fertilizer — is real too.

Iulia Blagu, a Romanian cereal farmer, described looking out at unharvested fields, “at the mercy of God and the climate,” because the crops can’t be stored or transported.

“And then you have this entire transit of Ukrainian cereals coming towards our country,” she said. “I mean … how can we handle that?”

Ketrin Jochecová contributed to this report.

]]> en Tory conference 2026: What POLITICO reporters are watching for https://www.politico.eu/article/tory-conference-2026-what-politico-reporters-are-watching-for/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Sun, 04 Oct 2026 02:00:00 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9084746 BIRMINGHAM, England — Britain’s largest opposition party wants to show it’s still on the electoral pitch during an annual gathering that kicks off Sunday.

Despite Conservative Leader Kemi Badenoch consolidating her position and seeing improved personal ratings, the party is still far from its government heyday, and faces an ongoing challenge on the right from Nigel Farage’s populist Reform UK.

Here’s what POLITICO’s team of reporters will be watching for as the Conservatives gather in Birmingham.

U.K. Political Editor Dan Bloom

My biggest question for Badenoch’s speech at 11 a.m. Wednesday will be: can she end Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s honeymoon?

Since July, Labour has jumped to 26% in the polls while the Tories lag behind Reform on 19%. There will simply be fewer lobbyists and hangers-on than at Labour’s jamboree.

Badenoch will spend this week arguing that Burnham, with his crusade against “40 years of neoliberalism,” has ushered in the kind of classic left-right ideological fight that she relishes. Expect her to bang on about cutting welfare to fund defense — two weak points for Labour. And the self-described “badass Kemi” plans to be more abrasive than Burnham, who went out of his way not to attack anyone in his speech.

I reckon two things will decide if she can cut through: her personal brand, and how far she can differentiate the Tories from Labour and Reform (plus, well, her own party from 2024). She will try to paint the Tories as the party of fiscal responsibility but that’s a crowded marketplace. It’s worked for the Conservatives in the past but we aren’t in two-party politics anymore — though admittedly, the five-party split has become less dramatic since the summer.

There will be economic policy announcements but perhaps not on the scale of last year’s pledge to scrap stamp duty. Badenoch has talked about getting rid of inheritance tax but aides appear to be suggesting an announcement isn’t ready.

I can’t wait to see the peacocking by would-be candidates for a general election. Tory aides are shouting from the hills that they are on a “war footing” and candidate selection is ramping up. Some of the high-profile Tories who were rejected for being too centrist are swerving this year’s conference, but former West Midlands Mayor Andy Street will be prominent on the fringe. Critics complain that Badenoch has bulldozed the transepts off her party’s ideological church.

And, of course, I’d ask questions about a coalition. There is no love lost between the Tories and Reform but all recent polls suggest they would have to team up to have any chance of running a government. Will she pull any punches against Farage … or Restore Britain chief Rupert Lowe, whose vote-splitting might help her in the end?

Senior Foreign and Defense Correspondent Esther Webber

I’ll be really interested to see how the party is positioning itself against what we know so far about Ed Miliband’s agenda as foreign secretary — so whether there’s any dissent over new sanctions introduced by Labour on Israeli E1 settlements.

Miliband has just begun to signal a potentially more conciliatory approach to China as an alternative locus of power and investment versus the U.S., so I’ll be looking at whether the Conservatives think this is a weak point where they can redouble attacks on Labour.

There’s also the question of artificial intelligence regulation and which camp the Tories are situating themselves in. Will they agree with the government on the need for a globally coordinated effort, or back U.S. President Donald Trump’s zero-regulation stance?

Finally, here’s a side plot: Are there any signs that former Home Secretary Priti Patel, traditionally a conference fan favorite, is actually doing anything in her new role in coordinating cooperation between the Tories and other parties internationally?

London Influence Reporter John Johnston

With little detail so far about Burnham’s plans for business, and many corporate execs pondering if Farage’s Reform has hit its peak, this Tory conference will be a vital opportunity for the party to try and show it is building back towards being a credible alternative.

Since the 2024 general election, many businesses and lobbying firms have sent only a skeleton staff to Tory conference. But I’ve heard that extra corporate passes and tickets to the standalone Business Day have been snapped up in the last few months. So, attendance may be healthier — even if most still won’t be splashing out on panel events or exhibition stands.

Business leaders remain skeptical about the prospect of an early general election. But as the official opposition, the Conservatives have the potential to help industry shine a spotlight on concerns and push issues up the political agenda if one comes. At last year’s conference, many public affairs pros felt the Tories lacked the ideas, unity and leadership to do that. My focus this year will be figuring out if that assessment has shifted.

Energy Reporter Abby Wallace

The Conservatives have come a long way from the party that, in government, enshrined net-zero targets in law. Badenoch has been clear about the direction she wants to take the party in: ditching legally-binding climate targets and drilling for more oil and gas in the North Sea.

The party’s leader has even suggested that former colleagues who still support the target will not be welcome back on the Tory benches. I’ll be looking out for whether that U-turn at the top has fully filtered through the party.

While energy bills have surged on the back of war in Iran, the party has been pressing Labour ministers to prioritize cutting costs in the system. For the Conservatives, that means ditching some support for renewables and a bigger role for gas and nuclear in the future. I’ll be keeping an ear on whether there is any pressure from the opposition for ministers to intervene ahead of what will be a difficult winter of price rises too.

The future of the North Sea, including looming decisions on Rosebank and Jackdaw, will no doubt spring up on the fringes — especially after the Conservatives clinched the Aberdeen South by-election following a campaign focused on oil and gas drilling.

Financial Services Reporter Eleanor Myers

Andrew Griffith will be stepping up this party conference, having been promoted to shadow chancellor earlier this year to replace his more mild-mannered colleague Mel Stride.

Griffith was a bigwig in business before he entered parliament, and as a former City minister, I’ll be watching whether he focuses his ire on the prospect of Labour raising bank taxes in the budget, which is now less than a month away.

Griffith will make his big speech on how to get Britain growing again at 2 p.m. Monday. Growth was the favored buzzword of former Chancellor Rachel Reeves, and has been heartily adopted by her successor John Healey, although how to achieve it remains a challenge amid soaring debt and rising interest rates. I’m interested to see whether the Conservatives propose a solution.

Senior Technology Reporter Frank Hersey

This conference is a chance for Badenoch’s team to establish any sort of differentiation between Tory tech policy and that of the other parties. This has been getting harder as parties’ approaches have coalesced. Labour committed to a pro-growth agenda for AI under former Prime Minister Keir Starmer with planned regulatory reforms to match. Tory plans for a social media ban for under-16s were eventually (and reluctantly) grasped by Labour. The Tories were further hemmed in by Reform banking the low-tax, low-regulation space.

I’ll be looking to see if the party can get ahead in any policy areas or if it has to pick new ones to do so. Among all the parties, there’s perhaps most interest in what the Conservatives say on tech — as their policy ideas in this space are feeling overdue.

Senior Trade Reporter Sophie Inge

The fightback against Burnham’s pledge to explore closer ties with the EU is expected to continue in Birmingham, after Badenoch warned that Britain shouldn’t be “having arguments which started 10 years ago.”

Deputy Leader Alex Burghart has already pledged to “reverse” the Brexit reset, warning that plans for an agrifood deal with the bloc risk undermining the U.K.’s trading relationship with the U.S., among other countries.

]]> en 2 Iranians charged with alleged bomb plot against Britain’s Jewish community https://www.politico.eu/article/two-iranians-charged-with-alleged-bomb-plot-against-britains-jewish-community/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Sat, 03 Oct 2026 16:01:51 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9102125 Two Iranian men have been charged with terror offenses over an alleged plot to bomb Manchester’s Jewish community.

Rahman Salehi, 34, and Salam Ahmadyan, 36, appeared in a British court on Saturday on charges of preparing to commit an act of terrorism or assisting another to commit an act of terrorism.

Police said the two men, who were arrested last month on the eve of the Jewish holiday of Yom Kippur, had received material and instructions on how to make a bomb, identified targets and carried out reconnaissance ahead of an attack on Jewish targets.

They also said another man, likely in Iran, was in contact with them over the plot. The arrests followed a joint investigation by counter-terrorism police and the MI5 secret services.

The latest charges follow Prime Minister Andy Burnham announcing there were “strong indications” that Iran was involved in a suspicious incident linked to the RAF Fairford last week, which involved three vans parked strangely and a group of hooded, masked men near the airbase.

Britain’s deputy assistant commissioner for counter-terrorism Vicki Evans said the last week has “brought into sharp focus some of the wider threats being projected into the UK from Iran,” while adding the two incidents “are not connected in any way.”

British Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said both men had arrived to Britain via small boats in 2020 and 2023. One had been granted asylum and the other had an asylum application pending.

EUobserver https://euobserver.com Independent EU journalism Sun, 04 Oct 2026 13:04:20 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.1.2 Latvian PM holds onto power as Russia-Ukraine war shapes election https://euobserver.com/240937/latvian-pm-holds-onto-power-as-russia-ukraine-war-shapes-election/ Sun, 04 Oct 2026 18:00:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=240937 Despite its ordinary conduct, Russia's war still shaped Latvia's election in a new normal for Europe that most of us had hardly imagined just five years ago.]]> Russia might not have directly interfered in Latvia’s election, but the vote still showed how the Ukraine war was distorting European democracy.

Latvia’s VDD intelligence service did not detect any of Russia’s classic interference tactics in the run-up to Saturday’s (3 October) vote, such as a spike in disinformation, vote buying, or a manufactured security scare.

The centre-right prime minister Andris Kulbergs retained power with 35.8 percent of the vote, even if coalition-building might take a while.

And voters’ concerns included the cost of living and failing healthcare, in what also sounded normal.

But despite the ordinary appearances, Russia’s war in Ukraine still influenced the election in fundamental ways, in a strange new normal for Europe that most of us had hardly imagined just five years ago.

Some analysts say even small changes would add to current price pressures, but a giant gas glut is coming and might arrive sooner rather than later. ]]> The EU has decided to delay its methane regulation, and the reason is simple enough. 

Europe imports almost 90 percent of its gas, which makes it one of the most exposed buyers in the world. And the US-Israeli war with Iran has choked gas flows through the Strait of Hormuz. 

Making matters more complicated is the fact that Europe is still phasing out Russian gas, with a total ban on Russian overseas liquified gas due to be implemented next year.

So few were surprised when energy commissioner Dan Jørgensen told ministers in Dublin this week that he will propose delaying the import part of the regulation by a year to 2028, although member states and parliament still have to formally agree.

]]> [Interview] ‘Putin understands only strength’: EU envoy in Kyiv urges stronger air defences and hybrid-war response https://euobserver.com/240045/interview-putin-understands-only-strength-eu-envoy-in-kyiv-urges-stronger-air-defences-and-hybrid-war-response/ Sun, 04 Oct 2026 08:55:40 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=240045 Katarína Mathernová, the EU's ambassador to Ukraine, says Putin is boiling Kyiv 'like a frog', but she is determined to stay. She sees parallels between Hitler's Mein Kampf and Putin's essay which stated that Ukraine has no right to national existence, sovereignty or identity. ]]> Ukrainians want peace more than anything, but only the language of strength works on Putin, says Katarína Mathernová, the EU’s ambassador to Ukraine.

Mathernová has no doubt about the Russian leader’s ultimate goal; she is convinced that Putin wants to destroy Ukraine.

“He set this out very clearly in his essay, and that is precisely why he launched this full-scale war. Unfortunately, the peace that Ukrainians so desperately want can only be achieved by putting pressure on Russia. Putin understands only one language — the language of strength,” she said in an interview.

Air raids have left their mark on her office: windows have been blown out, and shrapnel once tore straight through a refrigerator. With attacks intensifying, the EU delegation now does much of its work in the corridor, away from the glass. The latest strikes hit the nearby headquarters of Ukraine’s Security Service (SBU).

In late September, Kyiv has heard so many air-raid sirens. There is already one dead and 20 injured, and on our way to your office, we heard several explosions. Is this the new normal?

Unfortunately, they have become routine. It began on 27 August this year, a date that will go down in the history of this war. That day, we had 13 air raid alerts during daylight hours, a record since the beginning of the full-scale war. It happens every day.

The day before yesterday, as I was entering the office when the windows suddenly began to rattle. A huge plume of smoke rose behind that black building outside the window. There were around four separate explosions over the course of 20 minutes, just a couple of hundred metres from here.

The Russians have begun using jet drones which Ukrainians are not yet able to shoot down in the same numbers as earlier Shahed drones. With just a few jet drones, Russia can terrorise a city like Kyiv throughout the day at a relatively low cost. Then, at night, come the ballistic missiles. Last week, however, they also used ballistic missiles during the day.

Do the attacks make you anxious?

Of course they do. One morning last week, I was Nordic walking in the botanical garden. I was walking with my coach when suddenly there was a huge bang. It landed several kilometres away, but because there are no buildings there, it sounded as though it were just around the corner. These are the moments when I nearly have a heart attack…it’s very unpleasant.

How do you decide whether to go to a shelter or into the corridor? Do you have a security protocol?

Under Orbán’s government, relations had fallen to a historic low, raising the prospect of escalation. In June, Magyar announced that he had reached an agreement with Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky on settling the rights of the Hungarian minority in Transcarpathia, hailing it as a historic deal.

Since June, however, Hungary has repeatedly blocked Ukraine’s EU accession negotiations, arguing that progress on settling the rights of Hungarians in Transcarpathia has fallen short of expectations.

Domestic Hungarian politics can explain the dispute.

MOL, an oil company, signed a memorandum with Ukraine’s Naftogaz at the C8 meeting on the possible establishment of Ukrainian oil storage facilities in Hungary.

What is the Carpathian Eight?

In August, Zelensky announced the creation of the C8 to bring together countries from the wider Carpathian border region. The Ukrainian president said its members would focus primarily on the economy, security, the environment and investment.

Ukraine described it as a project intended to strengthen cross-border cooperation even with countries that do not provide it with military aid. Alongside Ukraine were to be Romania, Serbia, Poland, Slovakia, Czechia, Austria and Hungary.

Michal Lebduška, an analyst at the Association for International Affairs in Prague (AMO), said that it was one of many regional initiatives. While he did not believe it would trigger “major cooperation”, it could nevertheless be important.

On the other hand, the remaining countries sent lower-ranking representatives. Slovakia’s PM Robert Fico had initially indicated that he would attend, and was originally due to meet Tusk. At the last minute, however, he announced that he could not attend the summit due to sudden illness.

Slovakia was ultimately represented by Marek Eštok, state secretary at the foreign ministry.

Andrej Babiš’s Czech government all but completely ignored the initiative. As Respekt magazine wrote, Babiš declined the opportunity to visit Ukraine and did not send any representative to Bukovel.

So Czechia was represented at the summit only by opposition deputy Senate president Jiří Drahoš.

The release includes “a frontloaded substantial diesel release within the first 20 days,” a press brief released after a Friday afternoon call read.

The call was initiated by French president Emmanuel Macron who holds the rotating G7 presidency on Friday, after he spoke to US president Donald Trump on Thursday.

“Europe has just agreed to release a massive amount of their heavily stocked Diesel Oil. The process will begin immediately,” Trump wrote on Truth Social shortly afterwards.

Trump had pressured EU leaders to agree to the release all week.

On Thursday, US treasury secretary Scott Bessent urged Europe to “immediately” tap its reserves.

And EU leaders had received a proposal from the White Housethe same day for 120 million barrels of diesel over 180 days.

Washington had already approached France, Germany, Italy, Ireland and the UK individually, warning they could face US diesel export bans if they did not comply.

US diesel prices hit a record $6.53 per gallon last week, which is a liability for Trump’s Republicans ahead of the 3 November midterm elections.

Europe’s reward is a single line in the G7 statement, which reaffirms a commitment “to refrain from export restrictions on energy and energy products” between G7 countries.

The EU also on Friday had insisted that any further release come with a US pledge to avoid a unilateral diesel ban, and rejected the suggestion that they buckled to US pressure.

“We fully reject a [US] ban on diesel. A ban would not be beneficial to anyone. It would undermine our trust in the US as a reliable partner,” said Anna-Kaisa Itkonen, the commission’s energy spokesperson.

She declined to comment on the leader’s call ahead of time.

Commission chief spokesperson Paula Pinho said the coordination had “nothing to do with” recent threats.

She noted that gas prices had risen by 140 percent and diesel prices had doubled since February, and that a release agreed in March was still being implemented.

The G7 text presented Friday’s decision to release the 100 million barrels as continuing those commitments.

But the commission’s own oil coordination group concluded this week that there was “no immediate security supply issue” in the EU, Itkonen said.

Emergency stocks exist to deal with supply disruptions, not prices.

But the IEA route gives European capitals political cover, allowing them to present the release as collective action rather than a concession to Washington.

And it may not be the last one. “We will convene in the context of the IEA in the coming days to discuss the possibility of additional diesel releases as necessary,” the G7 statement said.

    The next legislative step was therefore expected to address one of the Union’s most pressing social challenges. The proposed Affordable Housing Act is an important step in that direction. Yet its binding Regulation focuses primarily on one specific aspect of the problem: restrictions on non-primary housing use, particularly short-term rentals, in areas under housing stress.

    While addressing short-term rentals is a welcome intention, it cannot on its own provide a comprehensive response to Europe’s housing crisis. 

    The pressure that holiday homes and short-term rental platforms are putting on housing markets, particularly in popular tourist destinations, has been rising, and giving local authorities better tools to respond is important. However, questions have already been raised about whether the proposed framework will give cities sufficient room to act effectively.

    For instance, the proposed approach to defining “areas under housing stress” risks being too narrow. Housing stress cannot be understood through property prices, income levels and short-term projections alone. Energy poverty, combined housing and energy costs, overcrowding, vacancy rates and the condition of existing housing stock all influence whether households can access decent and affordable homes. A broader understanding of housing stress would better reflect the reality facing communities across Europe.

    Yet the broader picture reveals an important limitation: many of the structural drivers of housing unaffordability remain outside the scope of the binding Regulation. In particular, it gives limited attention to one of Europe’s most significant untapped housing resources: the buildings and homes that already exist.

    Renovation, adaptive re-use and the mobilisation of vacant and underused buildings feature in the European Affordable Housing Plan and the Recommendation accompanying the Act. But if Europe is serious about increasing affordable housing stock, these approaches should play a stronger role in the framework itself.

    Across the EU, more than 47 million dwellings are estimated to be unoccupied. This does not mean that every empty home can or should be brought back into use. But it illustrates the scale of an existing resource that cannot be ignored. Bringing even a fraction of suitable vacant and underused stock back into use could create much-needed homes while reducing pressure for new construction and making better use of existing buildings and infrastructure.

    Europe cannot reuse buildings it cannot see. Yet many public authorities still lack reliable information about which homes and buildings are vacant, why they are empty, what condition they are in and what potential they have for affordable housing.

    The EU does not need to start from scratch. The Energy Performance of Buildings Directive (EPBD) and National Building Renovation Plans already provide a natural policy framework for understanding and planning the future of Europe’s building stock. Vacancy identification, mapping and monitoring should become part of the binding architecture of the Affordable Housing Act, ensuring that public authorities are, at a minimum, equipped to identify vacant and underused homes and assess their potential for conversion into decent and affordable homes.

    Identifying vacant buildings, however, is only the first step. The accompanying Recommendation could go further by providing guidance on how to mobilise vacant properties, support the conversion of different building types and develop viable financing models.

    EU financing should also better support the mobilisation and re-use of existing buildings. The next EU budget should continue to support affordable housing investment and recognise that renovation and re-use projects simultaneously deliver social, climate and energy benefits.

    Ultimately, however, success cannot be measured only in buildings renovated or investment mobilised. It must be measured in whether people can access decent homes they can afford.

    According to the Commission’s EU Anti-Poverty Strategy, one in five Europeans – nearly 93 million people – are at risk of poverty or social exclusion, while approximately 1 million people experience homelessness. Affordable housing policy must therefore place particular emphasis on those least well served by the housing market, including lower-income households and people experiencing or at risk of housing exclusion.

    The Affordable Housing Act is an important step forward. But as it moves through the legislative process, there is still an opportunity to broaden its ambition. A stronger focus on re-use, better implementation support, dedicated financing and a more people-centred approach would help turn a useful regulatory framework into a more comprehensive response to Europe’s housing affordability challenge.

    But from a legal point of view, EU countries can’t simply reintroduce border controls whenever they want.

    The Schengen area is based on the principle of free movement, meaning there should normally be no checks at internal borders. The Schengen Borders Code provides an exception.     His argument is that none of the migrants who arrived in Ceuta were transferred to Italy. And, he says, people travelling between Ceuta and mainland Spain are already subject to identity checks.

    So Austria is not checking passengers arriving by air from Spain.

    Germany, for example, has invoked the same exception in the Schengen rules to carry out controls at its land borders with all its neighbours.

    That does not mean that every border crossing is closed, or that every traveller is systematically checked. It means German authorities can carry out checks at those borders, including spot checks.

    So what’s the difference? First of all, OpenAI, Anthropic and Google have also signed the EU code, while Meta, SpaceX and Nvidia have not.

    And, more importantly, the EU does have binding rules in place: the AI Act, which is already in force. As part of this regulation, the European Commission developed the Code of Practice to help companies comply with the rules.

    You could think of it as a checklist for AI companies, to help them make sure they are complying with the law.

    Read more

    Let’s not allow AI firms to use fears of future dystopias to distract Europeans from existing problems

    Another difference is the sheer volume of recommendations. The document published by Trump is just one page long. The European Code of Practice runs to more than 60 pages and was prepared with the help of dozens of independent experts.

    It is also more comprehensive, covering not only safety, but also transparency and copyright. But this raises another question: if both documents are voluntary,  how effective can they actually be?

    When the European Code of Practice was published, some civil society organisations criticised it, arguing that voluntary commitments are not enough and that concrete obligations are needed.

    Read more

    EU states urged to ‘go beyond’ AI Act to protect people from abusive surveillance

    There are binding obligations under the AI Act. But they are not as precise as what is in the code of conduct.

    Similar criticisms have emerged since the White House agreement was published on Tuesday. And it is worse in the US case, since companies are absolutely not legally bound by the commitments they have made.

    The United States has generally been less inclined towards binding regulation of the sector. Trump has argued that rules can hinder the development of companies, and has promoted a national framework that is as minimally restrictive as possible.

    The White House document does leave the door open to legislation in the future. It says that, over time, it may make sense to codify these steps into lows or regulations.

    But for now, they remain voluntary commitments. If you are interested in this topic, there will be a live event on Tuesday next week about AI and its safeguards, organised by VoxEurope.

     It will be online and you can find all information on Vox Europe website. 

    ]]>         EU accession of Moldova and Ukraine is alternative to Nato, as Russia draws new Iron Curtain in Europe https://euobserver.com/239313/eu-accession-of-moldova-and-ukraine-is-alternative-to-nato-as-russia-draws-new-iron-curtain-in-europe/ Thu, 01 Oct 2026 10:03:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=239313 With Nato doors closed to Ukraine and Russia pushing a new Iron Curtain across the Black Sea, an “urgent” EU expansion toward Kyiv and Chișinău is emerging as Europe’s main tool to defend its eastern flank and preserve its global clout. ]]> “What is remarkable is that Ukraine and Moldova, despite finding themselves in a very tense situation regarding their security, are extremely keen to move closer to the EU and have therefore already begun negotiations and opened the first cluster.”

    These are the words of the deputy director of the European Council on foreign relations (ECFR), Vesela Cherneva, and they come just as the official negotiation process for the two countries’ accession to the European Union has begun.

    With this, the EU embarked on a truly geopolitical enlargement – driven not only by the pursuit of shared values, a larger market, and stronger common institutions, but also by the need to safeguard the continent’s security in a shifting environment.

    Ukraine: a battle-hardened nation’s journey from the post-Soviet world to the EU

    According to Cherneva, the EU’s upcoming enlargement is the only way to institutionally anchor Ukraine within a serious and lasting framework, given that the US position has remained clear under both presidents Donald Trump and Joe Biden: Nato enlargement to include Ukraine is not possible.

    “Currently, EU membership is the only way to integrate Ukraine’s and Europe’s security systems. This is an entirely different discussion from negotiations on chapters, clusters, sanitary standards and other accession requirements. We are talking about security guarantees, but also about the transfer of military technologies from Ukraine to Europe and, more broadly, about how Ukraine – which currently possesses the strongest and most combat-capable army in Europe – can, while defending Europe, also become part of the European security debate,” Cherneva says.

    Ognyan Minchev, political scientist, professor and executive director of the Institute for Regional and International Studies, an independent think-tank in Bulgaria, also believes that Ukraine’s importance is substantial and that the questions surrounding its integration are highly complex.

    “Ukraine currently possesses the only genuinely combat-capable army on the European continent. Western European armies have very limited personnel numbers and, until recently, received extremely low levels of funding. The lack of real resources, including weapons, to address the challenges of military security makes Ukraine a more attractive partner,” he says.

    Although many experts would point to Ukraine’s contribution to European security as the greatest benefit of its accession to the EU, the country can also contribute to development in other areas. There is undoubtedly great potential for development in the fields of agriculture and farming.

    The country has a vast area of cultivated land and is among the world’s leading producers of a number of cereal crops such as wheat, maize, barley, rice, and others. It exports these products to third countries, and membership would increase the EU’s economic influence in these regions.

    Ukraine’s accession could also lead to cooperation between different sectors and result in an increase in meat and dairy production as a consequence of increased cereal production.

    Beyond agriculture, Ukraine’s pharmaceutical industry could offer the EU an opportunity to reduce its reliance on imports of generic medicines from China and various Asian countries. Thanks to its favourable climate, Ukraine also has great potential for various types of renewable energy.

    Deposits of gallium, rutile, graphite, magnesium ores, lithium and other minerals vital to the green transition could contribute to European production and help the EU compete with China.

    According to Minchev, integrating Ukraine represents a major challenge because it involves a large country that is institutionally weak, with high levels of corruption, poor economic organisation and significant shortcomings in the functioning of public life.

    Read more

    What JK Rowling’s Voldemort can teach us about Ukraine war

    “Ukraine has been forced to transform itself into an effective fighting machine, but in other respects it remains a post-Soviet society with serious problems in the areas mentioned above. This makes its rapid integration into the EU extremely difficult,” Minchev says.

    Moldova: a key piece in Europe’s security architecture continues to struggle under Russia’s shadow

    “For Moldova, we can say that it is a small but significant element in the broader domino effect of Black Sea security, which is becoming an increasingly crucial aspect of overall European security. This is because the confrontation between the Kremlin regime and Europe is effectively unfolding along the line of a new Iron Curtain being formed across Ukraine and the Black Sea region,” Minchev says.

    According to Cherneva, Moldova’s accession is also crucial precisely because the country is a buffer state, and Russia has demonstrated that it does not tolerate buffers.

    Read more

    [Interview] Moldova races for EU membership by 2030: ‘We owe this chance to Ukrainians’, minister says

    “Russia seeks to conquer and control such buffer zones. If Moldova does not want to share the fate of Belarus or Georgia, it must take rapid steps towards European integration,” Cherneva says.

    For years, Moldova has served as a testing ground for Russia’s hybrid warfare. As Western European countries are only now confronting the full scale of Russian hybrid attacks, Moldova has already spent years developing its own resilience and countermeasures.

    The country brings to European security valuable expertise gained from combating Russian disinformation and resisting repeated attempts by the Kremlin to interfere in its domestic political processes.

    Yet Moldova’s accession would have implications extending far beyond security. Although it possesses far less agricultural land than Ukraine, the country has the potential to make a meaningful contribution to the European agricultural sector. Moldova has been gradually integrating into the EU’s Single Market through the Deep and Comprehensive Free Trade Area (DCFTA).

      <title>MS Now connects ‘blue dots’ at Texas fan event: ‘I always feel hope when I watch them’</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/media/2026/oct/04/ms-now-fan-event-texas</link>
      <description><p>Network at receiving end of White House press ban recently chose red state to host fan event as part of broader outreach</p><p>In 2024, Donald Trump and JD Vance carried Tarrant county, Texas, by 42,125 votes. So why, on the afternoon of 26 September, was the arena at the University of Texas-Arlington filled with nearly 5,000 super fans cheering for liberal media darlings Rachel Maddow and Lawrence O’Donnell like they were rock stars?</p><p>After two years of hosting the network’s annual fan event in dark blue New York City, MS Now (formerly MSNBC) got wind that something was happening in Texas. The state, which hasn’t elected a Democrat to the US Senate in 37 years, might do so next month, when 37-year-old James Talarico, Texas state representative, goes up against the Republican nominee, Ken Paxton, a well-known but controversial figure who ousted incumbent John Cornyn in the party’s primary with Donald Trump’s backing.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/media/2026/oct/04/ms-now-fan-event-texas">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <title>The American dream remains elusive in the valley that inspired East of Eden</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/03/salinas-california-john-steinbeck</link>
      <description><p>John Steinbeck’s hometown of Salinas is the least affordable city in the US for the middle class, a recent Brookings Institution analysis found </p><p>Nestled between two mountain ranges at the crook of central California’s coastline sits a valley known as the “salad bowl of the world”.</p><p>Farm workers stoop over neatly lined rows of crops off Highway 101 to harvest more than half of the nation’s supply of lettuce and nearly a third of its strawberries. The soil here is so rich that author John Steinbeck made the Salinas valley the promised land in his literary depictions of people chasing the American dream: immigrants, farm workers, westward-moving hopefuls, hungering for a better life.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/03/salinas-california-john-steinbeck">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <title>US added just 29,000 jobs in September in sharp drop from last month’s gains</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/02/september-jobs-report</link>
      <description><p>Final jobs report before the midterm elections also shows the US unemployment rate rose slightly to 4.2%</p><p>US employers added just 29,000 jobs in September, a sharp drop from last month’s gains, and unemployment rose slightly to 4.2%, a sign of a cooling labor market in the final jobs report before the midterm election.</p><p>The numbers were under half of economists’ expectations of <a href="https://www.wsj.com/economy/jobs/adp-says-private-sector-hiring-picked-up-in-september-d8c0f59e">just under 70,000 new jobs</a>. Most job gains were concentrated in the healthcare industry, which added 17,000 new jobs, while the information, financial and professional industries saw losses, according to the latest data from the US Bureau of Labor Statistics.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/02/september-jobs-report">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/australia-news/2026/sep/29/further-interest-rate-hikes-could-devastate-property-market-without-easing-unaffordability</link>
      <description><p>With RBA predicted to lift cash rate for fourth time this year on Tuesday, experts warn a fifth – or even sixth – rise would be ‘overkill’</p><ul><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/australia-news/live/2026/sep/29/treasurer-jim-chalmers-reserve-bank-cash-rate-decision-coalition-one-nation-ntwnfb">RBA interest rates live updates: cash rate announcement today – latest</a></p></li><li><p>Get our <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/email-newsletters?CMP=cvau_sfl">new political email</a>, <a href="https://app.adjust.com/w4u7jx3">free app</a> or <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/australia-news/series/full-story?CMP=cvau_sfl">daily news podcast</a></p></li></ul><p>Two or even three more Reserve Bank interest rate hikes would be “devastating” for the property market but still leave housing more unaffordable than ever as higher borrowing costs trump lower prices, experts say.</p><p>The RBA’s monetary policy board is widely expected on Tuesday afternoon to announce <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/australia-news/2026/sep/28/rba-expected-to-hike-cash-rate-to-46-its-highest-level-since-2011">an increase in its cash rate</a> to 4.6%, from 4.35%, in a decision that will add another $100 to the monthly mortgage interest bill on a $700,000 loan.</p><p><strong><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/australia-news/2026/aug/28/politics-really-newsletter-guardian-australia-free-best-daily-auspol-email-subscribe?CMP=copyembed">Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here</a></strong></p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/australia-news/2026/sep/29/further-interest-rate-hikes-could-devastate-property-market-without-easing-unaffordability">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <title>Financial bullying can ruin a marriage: first-person stories</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/money/us-money-blog/2014/aug/14/relationships-finances-bullying-abuse-dependent-equality</link>
      <description><p>When partners consider finances, when is it ‘my’ money, and when it is ‘our’ money? Guardian readers shared their experiences </p><ul><li><a href="http://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle/2014/aug/08/end-loveless-marriage-financially-dependent">Private lives: ‘I want to end my marriage but I’m financially dependent</a>’<br></li></ul><p>A survey of about 1,000 Americans found that one in 10 would describe their partner as a financial bully. Our readers, however, insist that that might be a label easily assigned to a partner who is simply being financially responsible.</p><p>When we put out a call to out readers last week to see if any of them had similar experiences, we found that many of you wouldn’t define the actions described as financial bullying. Instead, <a href="https://www.facebook.com/theguardian/posts/10152614052646323">quite a number of you insisted</a> that keeping track of your partner’s expenses was simply budgeting and being financially responsible.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/money/us-money-blog/2014/aug/14/relationships-finances-bullying-abuse-dependent-equality">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <media:content width="140" url="https://i.guim.co.uk/img/static/sys-images/Guardian/Pix/pictures/2014/8/11/1407775970091/35614646-3560-440e-99c3-7e064e53eac8-2060x1236.jpeg?width=140&quality=85&auto=format&fit=max&s=7f5a95db55fecaf83cb9d468ccb2fa7e">
