Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.

A group of prominent Polish businesspeople have announced that they are investing in a project to develop small modular nuclear reactors being led by the country’s richest man, Michał Sołowow.

Among them are Rafał Brzoska, founder of delivery giant InPost, and Mati Staniszewski, CEO of ElevenLabs, a leading artificial intelligence firm.

The group is investing 500 million zloty (€114 million) in Sołowow’s Synthos Green Energy (SGE), which, together with 1.35 billion zloty from foreign investors, will secure the company’s financing for the next two years as it seeks to roll out BWRX-300 reactors in Poland, Central and Eastern Europe and the UK.

As a European SMR development platform headquartered in Warsaw, Poland’s energy security is of special importance to us.

We are proud to announce that today our founder, Michał Sołowow, unveiled a PLN 500 million investment by a group of leading Polish entrepreneurs in SGE’s… pic.twitter.com/J2SerVjIlG

— SGE (@SGE_Nuclear) September 30, 2026

The investment, which was formally announced at a business conference in Warsaw on Wednesday, comes as Sołowow seeks to expand his nuclear project beyond SGE’s troubled partnership with Polish state energy giant Orlen, where disagreements have delayed plans to build SMRs in Poland.

Alongside Brzoska and Staniszewski, the other new investors are Dariusz Gałęzewski, co-founder of drinks maker Oshee; Krzysztof Pawiński, CEO of food company Maspex; Michał Brański of media group Wirtualna Polska; and Michał Wypychewicz of ZPUE, the largest manufacturer of transformer stations in Europe.

“They invested their own private funds because they understood the problem and then believed in the concept and the solution,” Sołowow told Business Insider Polska.

 

SMRs, which are prefabricated in factories before being installed on site, are seen by their proponents as a fast and cost-effective way of installing nuclear capacity.

In July, SGE announced plans to build 14 BWRX-300 reactors with a combined capacity of 4.2 gigawatts (GW) across three sites in the UK, which it said would generate enough electricity to meet 11% of the country’s demand. The company also hopes to deploy up to 26 reactors across six locations in Poland.

The BWRX-300 is a 300-megawatt water-cooled small modular reactor. Construction of the first ever unit began in Canada in 2025, with completion planned for 2029 and commercial operation expected in 2030.

Synthos Green Energy, a firm owned by Polish billionaire Michał Sołowow, has announced plans to build 14 small modular nuclear reactors in the UK.

It says that the £35 billion project could deliver enough power to meet 11% of the UK’s demand https://t.co/YTMIzYERuJ

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 2, 2026

Brzoska said that developing SMR technology “is an investment in Poland’s future”, because without “reliable, predictable and competitively priced energy…it is difficult to talk seriously about further growth in industry, data centres, artificial intelligence, automation or modern logistics”.

Staniszewski, whose company recently received an $11 million investment from Poland’s state-owned National Development Bank (BGK) to establish an AI development centre in Poland, said lower electricity prices were important for the sector.

SGE notes that demand for electricity is set to rise 40% in Poland over the next 14 years, according to grid operator PSE. Electricity prices have risen rapidly in recent years and are now the second most expensive in the European Union in relation to the cost of living.

Poland has recorded the EU's third-fastest rise in household electricity prices this year.

The country now also has the bloc’s second-most-expensive electricity, when taking cost of living into account https://t.co/WNLdCfOP16

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 30, 2025

Poland remains the EU’s most coal-dependent country, with more than half of its electricity generated from coal. Over the past decade, however, the country has diversified its energy mix, with the share of renewable energy sources tripling to nearly 30% in 2025.

Poland plans to reduce its reliance on coal further, including through the construction of its first nuclear power plant (of the traditional type, not an SMR). The 3.75-gigawatt project is scheduled to be commissioned in 2036.

Sołowow has also been pursuing the deployment of SMRs in Poland through Orlen Synthos Green Energy (OSGE), a joint venture between SGE and state energy giant Orlen, Poland’s largest company, to develop BWRX-300 reactors in Poland.

OSGE is seeking a so-called contract for difference (CfD) framework, an agreement with a state that guarantees a fixed price for electricity and helps shield developers from market swings, covering 14 reactors at three sites.

Polish state energy firm Orlen has announced an agreement to build the country’s first small modular nuclear reactor (SMR).

It says Poland will be the first country in Europe to deploy an SMR developed by US-based firm GE Hitachi Nuclear Energy https://t.co/MPWXS3qZ1d

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 28, 2025

The project, however, has been delayed by disagreements between the two shareholders. Sołowow told Business Insider Polska that they reached an agreement last month that would allow construction of two reactors to move forward, but said he regretted entering into the partnership with Orlen.

“I find it deeply regrettable, because it is precisely due to Orlen’s unnecessary involvement that we are discussing this project in political terms, even though it is not a political project,” he said.

Activists in Poland have launched what they say is the world’s first delivery locker that provides women with abortion pills, access to which is normally tightly restricted.

They have placed the device opposite parliament in Warsaw, a location intended to send a message to the politicians who have made Poland’s abortion laws among the strictest in the world.

The locker (called an “abortomat” in Polish, combining the words aborcja, meaning abortion, and automat, meaning an automatic machine) has been launched by Women Help Women (WHW), a global organisation that provides “self-managed abortion”, and Abortion Dream Team (ADT), a Polish activist group.

They emphasise that the installation “is completely real [and] not an artistic performance”. It consists of 22 numbered lockers and a numeric keypad. Women who have contacted WHM seeking an abortion are given a six-digit PIN code that opens one of the doors, inside which is a package containing the pills.

Recipients can either take the pills at home or do so in a specially prepared space opened last year by ADT and where the locker is located.

 

The activists emphasise that such delivery mechanisms for abortion pills are particularly important in Poland because of the country’s highly restrictive laws.

Abortions are only allowed in two circumstances: if pregnancy is the result of a crime (such as rape or incest) or if it threatens the mother’s life or health. As a result, only 851 legal terminations took place in Poland last year.

However, activist groups such as WHW, ADT and Women on Web (WOW) say that they help tens of thousands of women in Poland obtain abortions each year through other means, in particular by providing pills.

But they face legal risks for doing so: assisting someone in obtaining an unlawful abortion is a crime punishable by up to three years in prison. In 2023, ABW activist Justyna Wydrzyńska was convicted of that offence. Two years later, the sentence was annulled on a technicality and a new trial was ordered.

Polish activist Justyna Wydrzyńska, who was convicted for providing abortion pills to a pregnant woman, has succeeded in having the conviction overturned on appeal.

Wydrzyńska’s conviction came after the husband of a woman she helped obtain abortion pills found them and reported the case to the police. However, although assisting a woman in obtaining an unlawful abortion is an offence, the woman who had the abortion is not criminally liable.

Poland’s inflation accelerated to an annual rate of 4.0% in September, up from 3.4% a month earlier, driven primarily by higher fuel prices amid the ongoing conflict in the Middle East and the end of Polish government subsidies that kept down prices at the pump.

The development means that inflation has now risen above the upper bound of 3.5% set by the National Bank of Poland (NBP), which aims to keep the figure at 2.5%, plus or minus one percentage point. Analysts say that an interest rate hike by the NBP is now more likely.

The new preliminary inflation figures from Statistics Poland (GUS), a state agency, show that prices in September were 4% higher than a year earlier, the fastest rise since June 2025. On a monthly basis, prices in September were up 0.7% from August.

The rise was caused in particular by the price of fuel for private transport, which was up 36.1% on a year earlier and 9.2% from the previous month. Energy prices also rose, with electricity, gas and other fuels up 4.9% year-on-year and 0.9% month-on-month.

To shield consumers from the energy crisis triggered by US and Israeli attacks on Iran, Poland has twice introduced temporary measures to curb petrol station prices, including daily price caps and cuts in VAT and excise duty. The system was in place from March to June and again during the the last two weeks of August.

The government has been under pressure from the opposition and opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki to reintroduce the subsidies. However, it argues that Nawrocki’s decision to block a proposed windfall tax on fuel companies makes the measures harder to fund

 

Food and non-alcoholic beverage prices provided some offset, falling 0.5% from a year earlier, although they edged up 0.1% from August. Analysts, however, expect food prices to rise later in the year to reflect lower agricultural yields.

According to GUS’s own estimates, also published on Wednesday, the grain harvest came in 5% lower compared to the last season. This will, in turn, “push the CPI index higher in the coming months”, wrote Erste Bank.

The breach of the upper end of the central bank’s inflation target and the 4% threshold could influence the stance of the NBP’s Monetary Policy Council (RPP), prompting it to hike rates, added Erste Bank analysts.

A Polish painting looted by Nazi Germany during World War Two, and which once hung in an SS officers’ club, has been returned by its owner, who donated it to the National Museum in Warsaw.

“History is coming home,” said culture minister Marta Cienkowska, celebrating the return of Alfred Wierusz-Kowalski’s Winter – Napoleon’s Retreat from Moscow, which she described as “one of the most significant wartime losses in Polish painting”.

Her ministry is responsible for seeking the return of tens of thousands of artworks and other cultural items that were looted during the war and remain missing.

Wierusz-Kowalski, who was active in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, was a renowned realist painter whose work often featured animals alongside people. His Winter – Napoleon’s Retreat from Moscow had, by the 1930s, become part of the collection of Andrzej Rotwand, a wealthy banker and industrialist.

In June 1939, it was featured in an exhibition organised by the Society for the Encouragement of Fine Arts in Warsaw, which occupied the building that is now the famous Zachęta National Gallery of Art.

However, the exhibition was brought to an abrupt end when Nazi Germany invaded Poland on 1 September 1939. The works on display, along with other items from the gallery, were seized by the occupiers, with many used to decorate the offices and apartments of German officials.

Winter – Napoleon’s Retreat from Moscow was displayed in a club for high-ranking SS and police officers located in Warsaw’s Blanka Palace. The same building also housed Warsaw’s German-installed commissioner, Helmut Otto, and mayor, Ludwig Leist.

 

No information has been released as to the fate of the painting in the immediate aftermath of the war. However, it eventually came into the possession of Ewa Tsonis, who has now handed it back.

Speaking at a ceremony in the National Museum in Warsaw, Tsonis said that her late father, Michał Stefan Koryzna, had purchased the painting in the 1960s from Desa, a major gallery and auction house, in the city of Kraków.

“I grew up with this painting. It was greatly appreciated and loved in our family,” she said. However, after recently conducting research into the painting’s history, she became aware of its provenance and notified the culture ministry.

Ewa Tsonis (right) alongside the painting with culture minister Marta Cienkowska (centre) and the director of the national museum in Warsaw, Agnieszka Lajus

Experts from the National Museum in Warsaw confirmed the identity of the painting, which remains in good condition and in its original frame. Tsonis then donated the work to the museum.

“Restitution is not possible without the cooperation of many people and institutions – both on the side of the state and on the part of the owners of the works,” said Cienkowska, who thanked Tsonis for her “incredibly responsible and civic-minded attitude”.

“Such attitudes are still rare but, because we constantly talk about restitution – we search for lost works and strive to recover them – we are increasingly approached by people who own lost objects and feel a sense of responsibility for cultural heritage.”

Cienkowska noted that the culture ministry has so far secured the return of over 920 works, with around 200 more restitution cases currently underway in 18 countries.

Germany has agreed to return to Poland a collection of 73 medieval documents that were looted during WWII.

However, that is still just a small fraction of the over 60,000 missing items listed in the ministry’s database of missing works, which includes seven further paintings by Wierusz-Kowalski.

Two other works from Rotwand’s collection – Italian Woman by Anna Bilińska and Mother with Children by Kazimierz Alchimowicz – were also hung in the SS officers’ club during the war and today remain missing.

Poland has in recent years stepped up efforts to secure the return of historical and cultural items looted during the German and Soviet occupations.

In 2022, it appealed to UNESCO for help in securing the return of cultural items that remain missing after being looted by Nazi Germany. It also launched a campaign seeking the return of thousands of items that ended up in Russia after the war.

City AM https://www.cityam.com/ London's Business Newspaper Sun, 04 Oct 2026 13:29:23 +0000 en-GB hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.0.6 https://www.cityam.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/app_launcher_icon_final_rounded.png?w=32 City AM https://www.cityam.com/ 32 32 213406410 Healey’s headroom ‘could wiped out by Iran war’ https://www.cityam.com/healeys-headroom-could-wiped-out-by-iran-war/ Sun, 04 Oct 2026 23:01:00 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2462799

Chancellor John Healey’s fiscal headroom could be entirely wiped out by the impact of the war in Iran as economists said the Office for Budget Responsibility could offer a more pessimistic view on the UK economy.  A central fiscal forecast by analysts at EY suggests that the Chancellor’s buffer against a borrowing target has fallen [...]]]>

Chancellor John Healey’s fiscal headroom could be entirely wiped out by the impact of the war in Iran as economists said the Office for Budget Responsibility could offer a more pessimistic view on the UK economy. 

A central fiscal forecast by analysts at EY suggests that the Chancellor’s buffer against a borrowing target has fallen to £11bn. 

If the war in Iran drags on until the middle of next year, economists said that the headroom could be entirely wiped out as a further £18bn would be slashed from the fiscal forecast. 

The different outcomes for public finances reflect the UK economy’s partial dependence on events outside of its own control. 

EY analysis indicated that relatively small changes in forecasts could throw the Chancellor’s plans off course. 

The £11.3bn estimate draws on expectations that the Strait of Hormuz, the trading route in the Gulf region that is critical for a fifth of global oil and gas supplies, re-open around the time of the Budget.

Under its adverse scenario where inflation hit six per cent and activity across the UK economy dramatically slowed down, Healey would stare down a deficit of £7bn in his current budget for 2029/2030. The fiscal rules state that day-to-day spending must be level or exceed by tax receipts in the third year of the OBR’s forecast window. 

Healey’s Iran war problem

Pessimism across various markets has deepened in the last week following a rout in global bond markets and elevated energy prices, as shown by oil prices hovering around the $100 per barrel mark. 

Alternatively, EY research also suggested that a fall in the unemployment rate could deliver higher earning growth, boosting tax receipts at an earlier point in time. This could deliver the Chancellor a rise in the headroom to about £40bn.

Mats Persson, EY’s macro and geostrategy analyst, said forecast judgment showed “how exposed the UK’s fiscal position has become to events well beyond its borders”. 

“Energy market disruption originating in the Middle East has fed through into inflation, growth and borrowing costs, and UK gilt yields have reached their highest levels this century.  

“The geopolitical backdrop may be outside the government’s control, but strengthening the supply side of the economy, such as by unlocking stronger productivity or creating the conditions for sustained business investment, would build capacity to help absorb external shocks. 

“That is a longer-term agenda than any single budget but will ultimately determine how much room future chancellors have to work with.”  

]]> 2462799Maurício Alencar Maurício Alencar Heathrow and housing: Griffith pledges ‘most ambitious deregulation project’ in generation https://www.cityam.com/heathrow-and-housing-griffith-pledges-most-ambitious-deregulation-project-in-generation/ Sun, 04 Oct 2026 21:00:00 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2462873

The Conservatives’ pick for chancellor has pledged to roll out the “most ambitious deregulation project in a generation” as he is set to say plans could cut £50,000 off the price of a new home.  Andrew Griffith, the shadow chancellor, will say on Monday say he will slash red tape for businesses across construction, supermarkets [...]]]>

The Conservatives’ pick for chancellor has pledged to roll out the “most ambitious deregulation project in a generation” as he is set to say plans could cut £50,000 off the price of a new home. 

Andrew Griffith, the shadow chancellor, will say on Monday say he will slash red tape for businesses across construction, supermarkets and nuclear energy if the Conservatives are voted in at the next election.

Griffith is set to tell party members that stripping back regulations would end delays in planning and “rejuvenate” the City of London as well as investment across the country. 

A list of policies announced on Monday include the abolition of the quangos Natural England and the Environment Agency, the replacement of various infrastructure project charges with a single levy, scrapping environmental standards on housebuilding, and the removal of the Extended Producer Responsibility – widely labelled a “packaging tax”. 

The reforms altogether would reduce the cost of living and the prices of homes. The £50,000 reduction figure is also enabled by a pledge to scrap stamp duty on primary residence, according to party analysis. 

The Bank of England previously suggested that the packaging tax added 0.5 percentage points to CPI inflation. 

In his speech, the shadow chancellor will also announce that the UK would leave the Aarhus Convention, an international treaty that grants the public rights to decisions that impact the environment, in order to advance the construction of nuclear energy plants and other critical infrastructure. 

Natural England and the Environment Agency would also be moved to a “streamlined regulatory landscape”, with powers to be passed to ministers in the Department for Environment, Food & Rural Affairs. 

Griffith’s Heathrow pledge

Griffith said the Tories were prepared to “tell the hard truths”. 

In a major announcement for the party, Griffith is also expected to say a Conservative government would do “whatever it takes” to get a third runway built at Heathrow Airport. 

Former London mayor Boris Johnson was a top opponent to the construction of the third runway. Mayor Sir Sadiq Khan has also argued against its construction on environmental grounds while Prime Minister Andy Burnham refused to endorse the project that was heavily backed his predecessors in Downing Street.

A policy paper on the third runway is expected to be presented to parliament within months for MPs to vote on.

Sir James Cleverly, who wants to be the Tories’ pick for the next mayoral election in the capital, appeared to back the runway’s construction in a recent interview with City AM although he said local communities should reap the benefits of the project. 

Heathrow officials have pushed for the government to back the third runway as they have argued that an expansion of Europe’s second busiest airport was crucial to Britain’s trading relationship with different nations rather than just London’s business interests. 

In his speech, Griffith will say: “Countries on the rise have the best infrastructure and connectivity to the world but our national hub airport is being held back. The next Conservative government will do whatever it takes to end the delays and boost capacity by backing the third runway.”

Griffith will also say that a simplification of the tax code would be a central “objective” for every Treasury minister in the next Conservative government. 

His speech has been backed by other shadow cabinet ministers and industry bodies, including the Food and Drink Federation and British Glass. 

Heathrow chief executive Thomas Woldbye also said he welcomed the “can do” atittude on the airport’s proposed expansion.

Kemi Badenoch has defended the triple lock pension as the “right policy” ahead of the Conservatives’ party conference this weekend. 

Badenoch said the triple lock, which is widely condemned as “unsustainable” across the political spectrum, ensured pensioners who had “contributed” were properly rewarded.

The triple lock pension ensures that the state pension rises by whichever is highest out of inflation, wage growth or 2.5 per cent. 

Economists from across the political divide have warned that the “ratcheting” effect that sees the state pension far outpace wage growth in the long term left public finances exposed. 

Last week, Andy Burnham said Labour would fight the next election on a promise to reform the triple lock pension so that it rose by 2.5 per cent or inflation each year and levelled with earnings growth over the long term. 

In interviews on Sunday, Badenoch responded to claims by now-frontbencher Katie Lam, who said in a leaked recording from the summer that the triple lock would have to be abandoned. 

Badenoch said: “The triple lock is our policy. We believe that this is the right policy for pensioners.

“That is what we have planned. That is what we have promised. There is nothing that has happened that has made me change my mind. That is our policy.”

Lam, who is the shadow communities secretary, said what the country would “l need in the end is an entirely new pension system”. 

“I just think the whole system as it stands can’t stand for very much longer,” Lam said in the leaked recording. 

Triple lock split

Burnham’s new pension policy has split the Tories. Former Brexit minister Steve Baker hit out at the party over an advertisement claiming that Labour would “cut” the pension. Burnham’s policy ensures that the state pension continues to rise each year. 

In 2021, shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith, who was then a backbencher, wrote an article saying that the state pension triple lock was “unfair” as pensioners could “gain from the misfortune of others”. 

“I hope that we can build consensus on what should not really be a subject of controversy but a sensible and pragmatic response to post pandemic management of the economy,” he wrote in Conservative Home. 

Several other former Tory frontbenchers have also privately attacked the triple lock pension in recent months.

Heading to Birmingham for the Conservative Party conference, Badenoch unveiled a new intellectual paper that would set out “Conservative principles”.

The paper, titled ‘The Right Way’ in a nod to Margaret Thatcher’s ‘The Right Approach’, set out principles of wealth creation, freedom and responsibility, abiding by the law, and individual liberty.

The Tory leader said governments should be judged on actions rather than

Badenoch said: “We promised lower immigration without a strategy for delivering it. Net zero was legislated for before we had an economically feasible route to get there. We left the European Union without the economic plan that should have gone with it. The path to failure was paved with announcements, targets and good intentions.”

]]> 2462869Maurício Alencar Maurício Alencar Britain’s second richest person leaves for Monaco amid tax bite https://www.cityam.com/britains-second-richest-person-leaves-for-monaco-amid-tax-bite/ Sun, 04 Oct 2026 08:49:59 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2462865

Britain’s second richest person has left Britain for Monaco where billionaires can avoid paying income tax, inheritance tax or capital gains tax, according to reports. David Reuben, who also partly owns Newcastle United alongside Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund, is joining his brother Simon in the principality, The Sunday Times reported.  The two brothers were [...]]]>

Britain’s second richest person has left Britain for Monaco where billionaires can avoid paying income tax, inheritance tax or capital gains tax, according to reports.

David Reuben, who also partly owns Newcastle United alongside Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund, is joining his brother Simon in the principality, The Sunday Times reported. 

The two brothers were second on the newspaper’s Rich List with a combined wealth of £28bn. 

They join a flock of billionaires exiting the UK in the last two years, including the hedge fund investor Chris Rokos and the Goldman Sachs executive Richard Gnodde. 

The reason for his departure is unknown.  

Several other rich Brits live in Monaco, including Sir Lewis Hamilton and INEOS’s Sir Jim Ratcliffe. 

Tax questions hang over wealth exodus

Lawyers and economists, including the likes of Stephenson Harwood LLP’s James Quarmby and Panmure Liberum’s Simon French, have linked the string of wealthy investors and high taxpayers leaving Britain to new HMRC rules introduced by the Labour government. Several surveys have suggested that Britain’s richest were considering leaving over a high tax burden.

Since mid-2024, the government has ended the non-dom tax regime, added VAT onto private school fees and raised capital gains taxes. 

Pressure from the Labour Party has demanded that Chancellor John Healey increased taxes on the richest, including by raising capital gains taxes. Last year, dozens of MPs asked Healey to introduce a wealth tax on assets worth more than £10m. 

Debates over tax have become a key dividing line between Labour and other parties. 

In research on Sunday, the Centre for Policy Studies, a left-leaning think tank, warned that rates in the UK were about the same as the European average due to the tax gap on social security contributions. 

Robert Colvile, a CPS chief who is advising the government on small business taxes, said there was a “myth” across economists and campaigners from the left that the UK had a lower rate. 

“We simply have a system whereby some entitlements funded through general taxation in other countries are funded differently here,” Colville said. 

“Once you take into account private pensions, student loans, elderly social care and so on, you begin to see the full picture.”

]]> 2462865Maurício Alencar Maurício Alencar Wetherspoon boss blasts Soho’s ‘barmy’ vertical drinking crackdown https://www.cityam.com/wetherspoon-boss-blasts-sohos-barmy-vertical-drinking-crackdown/ Sun, 04 Oct 2026 07:00:00 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2462772

JD Wetherspoon boss Sir Tim Martin has blasted Westminster Council’s “barmy” curbs on vertical drinking, which he said are “inhibiting business”.  Martin, the chairman of Britain’s best-known pub chain, has waded into a row over the Council’s restrictions on so-called “vertical drinking” in Soho and an effective ban on new pubs and bars in the [...]]]>

JD Wetherspoon boss Sir Tim Martin has blasted Westminster Council’s “barmy” curbs on vertical drinking, which he said are “inhibiting business”. 

Martin, the chairman of Britain’s best-known pub chain, has waded into a row over the Council’s restrictions on so-called “vertical drinking” in Soho and an effective ban on new pubs and bars in the area.

The Conservative-led council sparked significant backlash last month after publishing plans to discourage pub goers from drinking while standing up, instead advising landlords to offer a minimum number of seats and to encourage table service. 

The licensing guidelines, which came into force last Thursday, encourage pubs and bars in Westminster to “reduce the extent of [or] remove opportunities” for vertical drinking. 

Martin, one of the country’s foremost publicans, told City AM that he opposes these curbs.

“I think every so often you read something, and to quote U2 from one of their songs, I just don’t believe the news today,” he said.

“That is completely barmy. There’s a lot of people who do desk jobs. When they go out, they just want to stand up for an hour or two because they’ve been sitting on their backside all day. 

“So the idea that you say to pubs ‘you’ve got to sit down’ is mad. It also contravenes NHS advice [which] says to people, especially as they get older, don’t sit down too much. Stand up.”

Tim Barnes, deputy leader of Westminster City Council, said: “There are not, and never have been, any plans to ban vertical drinking in Westminster. Your right to stand at the bar of the Dog and Duck with a pint remains sacrosanct.”

The local authority has resolved to take steps to “better explain” terms like ‘vertical drinking’ he added. 

But the council’s new licensing policy, which has now come into force, has enacted the proposed curbs on vertical drinking. 

It says: “When considering new licence applications, discourage excessive drunkenness and encourage the provision of more seating in premises that serve alcohol for people to sit and enjoy a drink and order food by table service in place of open bar space that caters for high volume vertical drinking.”

Wetherspoon’s Martin said the curbs are an example of excessive regulation weighing on Britain’s pubs. He said: “My advice to Westminster Council is the same as Ronald Reagan’s advice for governments: ‘don’t just do something, stand there’.”

Pub rules ‘inhibiting business’

Westminster Council’s new licensing policy also includes an effective ban on new pubs and bars in the area, which includes Soho – famed around the world for its nightlife. 

The guidance sets out a presumption of refusal for planning applications for new pubs and bars in the West End of London, saying that they will only be approved “where applicants can demonstrate exceptional circumstances”. 

Martin said: “I think it’s too restrictive in Westminster now, so I think it’s inhibiting business. I think it’s better for the economy, better for pubs, if licensing laws are liberalized somewhat, as they have been in many parts of the country.”

London mayor Sadiq Khan has previously criticised Westminster Council for the new curbs, accusing local policymakers of “breathtaking arrogance”. 

He said: “By ignoring all those who oppose their plans and viewing hospitality in the heart of our capital city as a problem, they are letting down businesses, residents and our economy. They would rather see nightlife die than thrive.”

Some 81 per cent of respondents to a council consultation disagreed with its effective ban on new pubs and bars in the West End.

Westminster’s Barnes added: “The reality is there are serious issues acting as a drag on our hospitality industry.  A lack of investment in policing has left the Met objecting to many licensing applications over public safety concerns. 

“People struggle to get home from a night out when late night bus routes have been cut and overnight Tube services are non-existent during the week.   

“We’ve spent the summer taking feedback from residents, the hospitality industry and visitors. We’ll take this on board and do our bit to support the hospitality industry, but we need the Mayor’s team to fund the services which make London a 24-hour city.”

The BBC’s decision to drop lunchtime and overnight sports bulletins from its news channel has rightly had a few journalists loosening their collars. Savings must be found, but will people miss the content? It really reflects how crowded the race for sports audiences has become. Broadcasters used to be the thoroughbreds, with competitors left in their dust, but the gates have opened and half the runners no longer need a television commission.

Do people still watch sport bulletins? Anyone who follows football transfers spends more time on Fabrizio Romano’s social media channels than most of their relatives. And football fans will happily spend an hour listening to someone who knows their club down to the physio’s second cousin twice removed. Getting them to wait until lunchtime for an update, however, feels positively archaic when they have already spent the morning arguing about it on X.

Itchy trigger finger  

Live rights are still a formidable advantage. Broadcasters can pull millions of eyeballs onto a TV screen at the same time, with the scale and production expertise that blow independent channels out of the water. But the BBC are also bound to reach beyond the most zealous of fans. A YouTube channel has more editorial freedom and can home in on a niche with much less red tape than a mainstream broadcaster.

The golden question comes when that audience reaches for the remote once the game has finished. A scheduled bulletin offered convenience when catching up, in the same way post-match analysis could inherit the audience before it. Both now face viewers with too many options. The match still gives broadcasters a head start, but a remote can take you to another platform at the touch of a button or with a few dictated keywords.

And that creates an awkward imbalance for commercial broadcasters who carry the cost of showing the match, while someone else can build a following from discussing it. The rights still hold a value, but relying on them to carry a dated studio show can become expensive.

Branded YouTube shows like Betway’s ‘Settle It’ show how much there is to work with between games. Viewers follow talent and come back for their personality as much as the football, which gives sponsors a regular spot in fans’ lives without needing to buy broadcasting rights.

BBC change?

Broadcasters have every chance of building their own relationships; the BBC’s growing venture into YouTube is testament to that. But commissioning something for YouTube requires a willingness to let the audience have a bigger say. Taking a television format online with a younger presenter papers over some gaping chasms.

In television, a development team might hand over a format and move on once it is commissioned. Online, we recommend development producers stay much closer throughout the series.

A throwaway conversation might become the reason viewers return, while the segment everyone loved in the pitch turns out to be where they leave. There’s little sense in keeping it for another fifteen episodes just because it looked good in the deck.

More of the money around live rights should go into teams that can keep doing that work throughout a season. Broadcasters have paid dearly to bring everyone together and so they should have a decent chance of being the place those people choose to return to, even when there’s no match to show.

On the first day of the party’s conference in Birmingham, Badenoch will announce that the childcare cliff edge – engineered under the previous Tory government – will be scrapped at a cost of about £700m per year. 

Former Chancellor Jeremy Hunt created the cliff edge when he announced that parents on income under £100,000 could claim 30 hours of free childcare for under four-year-olds. 

The change in approach builds further distance between the current leadership and Rishi Sunak’s Conservatives that lost the election in 2024. 

Badenoch said the cliff edge was absurd” as earnings of just one extra pound above £100,000 could leave families worse off than those below the thresholds. 

“Conservatives believe that you shouldn’t be punished for working more, but this childcare cliff edge does exactly that,” Badenoch said.

“I’m a mum of three and I’ve had to make the same choices many families have had to make on work and childcare. Those choices are difficult already, government should not be making them harder.

Free childcare trap

The £700m costing is based on a recent report by the Centre for the Analysis of Taxation. 

Centax estimated that there are nearly 12,000 parents deliberately holding their income below the £100,000 threshold in order to get free childcare. 

Hunt introduced a state-funded childcare scheme in March 2023. The government is reviewing the success of his flagship policy. 

Centax analysts also said that one third of parents earning between £100,000 and £120,000 received free childcare through a loophole in the system.   

The Tories said they would also remove the cliff edge for tax-free childcare, which pushed up the costs slightly. 

Party officials said the cost would be covered by reversing the increase in the number of public servants in non-departmental public bodies, which would save about £1.6bn by 2030 according to the Conservatives.

“I’m trying to prove you can still have a great night out in Soho,” I say. “You can. But not a late one,” replies Lesley Lewis over a glass of white wine at her beloved pub the French House. “I’ve always loved Soho,” says the legendary proprietor, who has run the French House for 37 years. “I will love it until the day I die, and I don’t intend to leave. To me it’s a special, magical paradise. Back in the day everywhere used to be open till 3am. Now, it’s more… restricted.” 

At 71, her nights may not run so late these days, but she wants Soho to remain a place where people can come together and party until dawn. And she knows a thing or two about the Soho community. Her pub, a Soho mainstay since 1891 and once the haunt of legends like Lucian Freud and Francis Bacon, was kept alive during Covid by a crowdfunding campaign initiated by locals who couldn’t bear to see it shut. 

Can you party after 1am in Soho?

Today she says Soho’s late-night culture is being erased. People can still go out in Camden, she says with a roll of her eyes, but it’s getting harder and harder to keel onto the streets of Soho past midnight like Mick Jagger used to. “We need to open the clubs! Let people enjoy themselves. Let people dance!”   

Despite her concerns, I’m determined to prove that the birthplace of Cool Britannia is alive and kicking. That’s how I found myself at the Hippodrome Casino at 4.30am nursing a Diet Coke and an incoming headache, trying to remember everything that led to me sitting beside a man who’s fallen asleep at a slot machine. 

•••

My plan was simple – to embrace the best part of Soho: the people. At each bar, I’d ask someone where I should go next, and see where it took me.  

“In Soho, you’ll chat to people you wouldn’t normally,” says Eva, a bartender at the French House who says she’s ended up on wild nights out with people who came to the bar alone. There’s just something about the compressed energy of Soho that gets people chatting, she says. 

In fact, people are chatting so much at the French House that it’s making it hard to hear my friends – so much for Soho being ‘too quiet’. I turn to two other bartenders, both nursing red wines after their shifts, and ask them where I should go. 

They suggest Trisha’s down the street, so I turn on my heels (yes, it’s a heels kind of night) and head to my favourite red carpet: the one that leads down unassuming stairs to a bar that looks like it could play a pivotal role in The Godfather. 

‘It’s madness because it’s Trishas’

I weave past the gingham tablecloths on the small round tables and a giant picture of the eponymous Trisha and make my way towards the smoking section. Here I get chatting with Imran, who’s been behind the bar for six years. “Sometimes we get a lot of nutcases in here, like him,” he says, pointing to a regular standing beside us. “It’s madness… because it’s Trisha’s. I can’t say why it’s madness.”

Imran says there are too many chains coming into Soho, which are ruining its individuality. He worries that places like Trisha’s are dying out. When I ask him for Trisha’s lore he asks “are you still recording?” before shaking his head. For my next stop, someone at the bar recommends I check out a place called The Pink Flamingo on Brewer Street, so I head out into the night. Behind the bar at the Flamingo, Dave has a similar tale of woe. He says his bar, which is attached to the El Camion restaurant upstairs, used to be the moneymaker of the two, but now it’s flipped. People want to go out to eat rather than dance all night in a basement. 

He said the place used to be filled with students until 3am, but now fewer young people are taking their turn on the dance floor. I suggest the £14 drinks might have something to do with it but he says that’s the price of keeping a venue open in central London. It’s a never-ending cycle of rising prices and declining patrons. 

As someone who remembers the days when you could sneak into Soho bars with little more than a fake ID and a smile, I feel ancient in this student-heavy crowd, so I head to my next destination: Udderbelly. This is one of my favourite underrated Soho locations. You don’t need to go to the attached theatre to gain access to its affordable espresso martinis and watch a show on the mini stage, where on Saturday a drag queen was belting out her best Celine Dion impression. 

It wouldn’t be a trip to Soho without a minor celebrity encounter, and I spot Bridgerton star Luke Thompson. Buoyed by the confidence of three espresso martinis, I told him I was writing a story on Soho nightlife, and asked if he had any spots he’d recommend. He did not.

The Box is a legacy of debauched Soho

The bartender did, though: he said we should go to Raincall. I’m making my way there when my phone chirrups. Earlier in the day I’d messaged a guy who knows a guy. Now confirmation has come through: I’m on the coveted guest list for The Box.

The Box, for the uninitiated, is the infamous night club between Shaftesbury Avenue and Brewer Street that promises to keep alive the tawdry side of Soho. It’s extremely exclusive, only accessible to women with good contacts and men with deep pockets. It’s the kind of place where you have to look a certain way, wear a certain outfit, and speak a certain language to get through the doors, which feels a little removed from the free-spirited foundations of Soho’s nightlife of yore. 

The Box is as filthy as it’s always been: it’s notorious for its hourly stage shows where you can see everything from a ‘doctor’ giving a ‘patient’ a transplant by pulling a heart out of their behind, to someone shooting ping pong balls across the room using only the power of their vagina. It is a little frustrating that this is the only place in Soho open until 4am (and its licence to sell booze ends at 3am). 

Don’t get me wrong, however: I still get a thrill from dancing on tables and being handed glass after glass of free Dom Perignon. You can party until the small hours in Soho, provided you have the right connections…

In Soho, a tension is brewing

While Soho feels like a congenial place when you’re sharing cigarettes and enjoying half-remembered conversations with strangers, in the broad light of day tension is brewing. 

According to the Home Office, only 16 out of 41 licence applications were granted in the West End between 2023-24, and applications for new pubs and wine bars fell by 80 per cent between 2022-24. 

I meet Westminster council’s deputy leader Tim Barnes, the Conservative councillor for Soho, for a coffee at – where else? – Bar Italia on Frith Street. He disputes the idea that there’s no night life in Soho. “It just isn’t true… you’ve got plenty of pubs and bars, depending on what night of the week it is, that are open until 1am.” 

But this isn’t about 1am, I say, this is about 3am and beyond. Soho was once the centre of the most vital cultural capital in the world. Today there’s hardly anywhere to party until dawn. A case in point: one of my favourite spots, Helen of Troy, used to be open past 3am in the 1970s but now has a hard kick-out time of 2am.

Barnes says it’s not that people are looking for late-night activities and can’t find them: it’s that fewer people are going out late to begin with. They are drinking less, he says, and there’s a lack of late-night transport. But this doesn’t quite wash: the underground runs 24 hours a day over the weekend and there are plenty of warehouse venues across London that are far less accessible than Soho. If people can get back from Venue MOT in Surrey Quays at 4.30 in the morning, surely they can get back from Dean Street?

The lack of late venues isn’t a London problem – it’s a Soho problem. I go out in Dalston most weekends and you can roll out of a basement at 3am straight into a kebab shop that’s more rammed than the club. The same goes for Peckham, Brixton, Hackney Wick… 

‘Fewer places open late than ever’

But in Soho, there are fewer places than ever that are open late – I should know, I just stayed out all night trying to find them. After leaving The Box, I asked around to see what my options were. “Not much,” was the consensus. “You could try the casino,” hazarded one staff member, who I’m sure just wanted rid of me. That’s how I ended up in a windowless room sitting beside a man slumped across a one-armed bandit.

Surely some of the blame must lie at the hands of Barnes and his peers, especially in light of their much-lampooned stance against what they called “vertical drinking” – standing up, to you and I – which could further exacerbate Soho’s lack of late night options. Barnes counters that the police are often responsible for licences being rejected, not the council. But when I spoke to the Met they said they only offer advice – local authorities make all the decisions. Nobody wants to shoulder the blame.

Barnes is undeterred: “When you say, ‘What’s Soho about now’, I think it’s going back to being on the frontline of culture. It hasn’t really known what [it was] for the last 20 years. Now places [like Trisha’s] have swung around from being old and out of date to being kitsch to being something of their own. The circular nature of sh*t has kicked back in… There’s more culture and music and art, there’s a whole massive explosion of that which is so f*cking brilliant.” 

What’s f*cking brilliant is being in The Box and seeing a fully naked woman whipping a whisky sour around with her plait, or meeting a lady in her fifties in the bathroom who has been going there her whole life and has no plans to stop, or running across Shaftesbury Avenue at four in the morning with a man I met outside a closed Bar Italia who calls himself “The King of the Road.”  

What’s not so f*cking brilliant is that, while there are places to go in Soho past 1am, you either have to know a guy or have near-unlimited funds. Places like The Box and Soho’s myriad members’ clubs are doing just fine, but nightlife here has always been built off of queer, audacious events that were welcoming to anyone freaky enough to give them a go. Now they’re hidden behind layers of social privilege and wealth. 

That’s why I take going out so seriously. Every tequila shot taken in a sticky Soho basement is a socio-cultural choice. There are plenty of quiet areas of London. Soho should not be one of them. In the words of Lewis: “Let’s just dance. It’s all we want to do.”

Professional sports teams, governing bodies and operators of stadiums and events could all face legal action if players receive abuse due to changes in the law this month, writes Charlotte Smith.

Sports organisations have historically treated abusive behaviour directed at players, coaches and officials largely as a welfare, reputational and regulatory issue. However, from 1 October 2026, new third-party harassment provisions will create a significant employment law dimension.

Under the Employment Rights Act 2025, employers may be liable for harassment committed by third parties, including supporters, spectators and online audiences, unless they can demonstrate they have taken “all reasonable steps” to prevent it. The reforms will affect organisations across the sports sector, from professional clubs and governing bodies to event operators and sporting venues.

Sports organisations do not need to look far for examples of the harassment challenges their employees face. England footballers Bukayo Saka, Marcus Rashford and Jadon Sancho were subjected to racist abuse following Euro 2020, while Lionesses defender Jess Carter has spoken publicly about the abuse she received during Women’s Euro 2025.

In rugby union, the RFU increased sanctions for abuse of match officials after a survey found almost half (49 per cent) of referees had experienced abuse, highlighting the scale of the issue and concerns about retaining officials within the game. 

Cricket faces similar challenges. The Cricket Regulator reported receiving more than 200 reports of abusive messages in a single year, with female cricketers particularly targeted and many messages linked to individuals who had lost money betting on the women’s game. 

These examples also demonstrate why the reforms have such broad implications. The new provisions are not limited to elite athletes but apply across the wider workforce that supports professional sport. 

From October, organisations could therefore find themselves facing scrutiny not only where a player is subjected to abuse, but also where a steward, hospitality worker, or any other employee experiences discriminatory or harassing conduct from supporters or visitors. 

What steps should sports organisations take to protect players?

What constitutes “all reasonable steps” to prevent harassment will vary depending on the organisation and the risks it faces. However, sports organisations should be considering the issue at board level, with the aim of fostering a top-down culture that promotes anti-discrimination and champions diversity and inclusion.

Risk assessments should be undertaken to identify where harassment may arise, whether on matchdays, in hospitality settings or through online channels, and used to inform appropriate preventative measures.

That may include reviewing ticketing terms and codes of conduct, strengthening reporting procedures, ensuring stewards and security staff are trained to respond appropriately to incidents, and considering how abusive or discriminatory content directed at players, coaches and employees is monitored and addressed. 

Clubs should also remember that workplace risks are not confined to the stadium. Media appearances, community engagement activities and other public-facing duties can all form part of the risk environment they are expected to manage.

Ultimately, organisations will need to be able to demonstrate not only how they respond to incidents, but also the proactive measures they have put in place to prevent harassment from occurring.

America, which is the world’s largest diesel producer, has threatened to curb or ban its exports of the fuel unless Europe taps into its reserves and relieves pressure on the supply-starved global market.

In a post on social media, Donald Trump said Europe had agreed to “release a massive amount of their heavily heavily stocked Diesel Oil”, adding that the process would “begin immediately”.

Alongside recent elevated oil prices, Iran and Ukraine have been targeting refineries in a move to hamper global refining capacity and ramp up strain on the global market.

Foreign secretary Ed Miliband represented the UK on the call with G7 members, according to reports, and was joined by senior leaders from every other G7 nation. In a statement after the G7 call, leaders said they had “agreed on decisive, coordinated measures to stabilise immediate energy supplies, shield households and businesses from price shocks, and strengthen the long-term resilience of global energy systems”.

One of London’s greatest assets is its varied and wide-ranging sports scene; six Premier League football clubs, many further down the pyramid; iconic rugby, tennis and cricket grounds; indoor arenas as far as the eye can see.

But with success comes a desire to expand and grow. Chelsea are actively assessing options for a new site to replace Stamford Bridge, Wimbledon is set to expand its tennis empire into a local golf course, and somewhere in the capital could soon be home to a 20,000-capacity basketball arena.

In a city that houses 9m people, land is limited. But seven sites spanning nearly 2,500 acres – 3,000 if you add in Stratford’s Olympic Park – are being developed, with mixed views on whether they could accommodate an arena.

By far the biggest development underway at the moment is in the west of the capital, where a 1,600-acre site will soon be home to HS2 (hopefully) and a monumental range of new residences and retail spaces. QPR had previously touted a stadium on Old Oak Common, but what about an NBA arena now? Well, it’s not clear. 

A spokesperson for the Mayor of London told City AM: “We look forward to working with them on any future plans to bring top-tier basketball to London.” It’s not a no.

A day, or 24 hours, isn’t really enough to experience any city in the world, let alone Athens, one of the world’s most historic and diverse cities.

That doesn’t mean you shouldn’t try. If you’ve only got 24 hours, a quick stopover between flights, or just want to get away for the weekend, you can make the most of this fantastic city and grab a snapshot of everything it has to offer.

Luckily, the Greek culture in Athens lends itself to long days.

How to plan your trip to Athens

The first thing to do (ideally a week before) is to book tickets for the Acropolis and Parthenon. If you’re planning on visiting these UNESCO World Heritage sites (and let’s be honest, that’s usually the main reason people visit Athens), booking a ticket to skip the line is essential. Shell out for the museum and audio guide, too.

Tickets are sold in one-or two-hour slots, letting you skip the line (although you’ll still have to queue, since everyone buys the tickets). Still, they guarantee a time slot, giving a anchor to plan the rest of the day, although it’s probably best not to try and squeeze in too much around the main event; you can get a flavour of the city with a few key sights.

What to see

The best way to see a city, any city, is to get right at it. Grab a pastry and coffee from a local bakery for breakfast. You’ll almost certainly discover something along the way.

Then jump on the metro. Greek traffic can be atrocious at best and you don’t want to waste 20 minutes stuck in a traffic jam on a 15-minute journey. The Metro takes contactless cards, or you can buy a 24-hour pass, which will get you across the city, or at least to the major sites, with relative ease.

Aside from the Acropolis, the Panathenaic Stadium is one of the city’s best landmarks. Dating back to the 4th century BC, it was originally built for the Panathenaic Games festival and entirely rebuilt in 1895 for the first modern Olympic Games of 1896. Buying a ticket should be considered optional – unless you’ve never been in a stadium before.

On the way from the stadium to the Acropolis, visitors can swing by the ruins of the Temple of Zeus – once the largest temple in Greece, dedicated to Zeus, the king of the gods – and the Arch of Hadrian (Hadrian’s Gate), both wonders of this ancient city. Before or after the main event, it’s also worth visiting Hadrian’s Library, just north of the Acropolis and the National Archaeological Museum, a 15-minute metro ride away.

A whistle-stop tour of Athens wouldn’t be complete without a visit to the Greek Parliament building on Syntagma Square. The changing of the guard ceremony is widely regarded as one of the best things to do in Athens, doesn’t require a ticket, and, because it takes place on the hour every hour, is often uncrowded.

Where to eat in Athens

Ending your sightseeing tour at Syntagma Square puts you in the heart of the city, and it’s the perfect place to hunt for dinner.

You’ll find the usual tourist fare, gyros, Greek salad, and Souvlaki, in most eateries around the square. But walk a few roads back, and you’ll uncover hidden wine bars, local restaurants and fine dining spots.

For upmarket souvlaki, there’s Meat the Greek, a ten-minute walk away from the Square. Heterclito next door, or Cherchez La Femme, also next door, are both open late are perfect spots for after-dinner drinks (or dinner and drinks at the same time).

For something a bit more upmarket, and a bit further away, there’s Thes. Billed as “Greek Creative Cuisine” it’s worth booking ahead. Then for the best ice cream in the city, Le Greche Syntagma, once again near the Square, has some of the most innovative and traditionally Greek flavours around.

Athens Hotels: Where to stay

Conrad Athens The Ilisian has transformed an iconic 1960s landmark into a world-class urban resort, combining luxury hospitality, private residences, and the exclusive House of NYNN club.

Located near, and with views of, the Acropolis and the National Gallery, the property features restored mid-century art, including Yannis Moralis’s signature marble façade.

Culinary experiences, led by two-Michelin-starred Executive Chef Angelos Lantos, feature Byzantino Grande Brasserie, Onuki, and the rooftop Galaxy Supper Club. Guests can enjoy the city centre’s largest outdoor pool, a 700-metre Green Roof running track, and curated retail spaces.

Rates at Conrad Athens start from €640 per night and include breakfast.

Firms’ inflation expectations for the next 12 months rose higher, according to closely watched Bank of England survey, the results of which could pile pressure on policymakers to raise interest rates. 

The Bank’s monthly survey of firms’ price expectations, the Decision Makers’ Panel, showed price expectations becoming more jittery as costs from the energy price spike could be passed on to consumers. 

One-year ahead CPI inflation expectations rose from about 3.1 per cent in August to 3.3 per cent last month. 

Longer-term inflation expectations and wage growth predictions also edged higher, according to research, reflecting the heap of price pressures building across the UK economy.

The majority of firms responding to the Bank data collectors said that higher energy prices were having a high impact on price-setting. 

A higher proportion of businesses also warned that uncertainty levels were very high, putting the UK economy on less steady footing. 

Figures from the survey heavily influence the Bank of England’s nine-strong committee of rate-setters ahead of crucial decisions on monetary policy. The next meeting for the Monetary Policy Committee is a month away and will come after Chancellor John Healey’s Budget. 

Interest rates pressure builds

Over the last week, several policymakers including governor Andrew Bailey, Clare Lombardelli and Sarah Breeden have cautioned that interest rates may have to be raised from 3.75 per cent if global energy prices remain elevated. 

On Friday, the Brent crude oil price, a benchmark for international prices, hovered around the $100 per barrel mark. Before war across the Middle East broke out in late February, prices were at under $70 per barrel, representing an increase of more than 40 per cent. 

The Bank’s main forecast suggests that inflation could top four per cent in the early months of next year. Both short-term and long-term UK government bond yields have risen. Bank member Catherine Mann has suggested that the Bank needs to raise interest rates to maintain credibility with markets.

On Wednesday, the Bank official Alan Taylor said rate-setters had to remain “vigilant” although he warned that interest rates did not need to “react mechanically” to energy markets. 

Taylor, who is seen as a more dovish member of the Monetary Policy Committee, pointed to the weak labour market and falling food inflation as showing that inflation may not rise as much as some economists fear. 

“Taken together, these developments suggest that the economy is proving less susceptible, at least so far, to a repeat of the dynamics seen in 2022,” he said.

Faltering demand, especially in the USA, has promoted concerns about oversupply and the prospect of another whisk(e)y loch. A number of Scotch distillers are slowing down production, but for Tom Bruce-Gardyne it feels like a bigger issue across the pond …

“Every drop of liquid we distil, every barrel we choose to fill, every palate that we make and move around the world has to work harder for returns on our capital.” This was the solemn pledge of Ewan Andrew, Diageo’s President Global Supply Chain & Procurement, at the company’s Capital Markets Day presentation that followed its full-year results on August 6th.

The current value of Diageo’s maturing stocks is put at $8.5bn, of which around two thirds is Scotch whisky. That represents a huge stash of casks slumbering in warehouses across Scotland, feeding the angels up above, and not exactly working hard. 

Ewan describes Diageo’s inventory as “a sizeable competitive advantage if it is deployed correctly.” But it seems it has grown too big. “We have scaled back production and distillation,” he told analysts at the presentation. “That’s been done across Scotch, North American whiskey and Tequila. We are at the minimum requirements for future blend and support of growth.” 

Judging by one of the graphs he displayed, there is to be a dramatic cut in production of about two thirds in this fiscal year, before a partial recovery through to FY29. In his words, compared to the past three years: “we are reducing our barrel by more than 50 per cent in the forward three-year cycle.”

How these cuts will fall between Scotch, North American whiskey and Tequila is unclear. We know that Diageo paused production at its third biggest malt distillery of Teaninich that has a 10m litre capacity last September, and did the same to its Roseisle maltings in November. Production at the company’s massive Cameronbridge grain distillery has also been reduced, leading to eight job cuts which has provoked the workers to go on strike. 

Paddy Fletcher, co-founder of the Port of Leith distillery, believes these production cuts are really to appease City investors who struggle to grasp the long-term nature of the industry, and are demanding that Diageo look at its free cash-flow metrics. “The only way to reduce your free cash-flow, is to stop making whisky,” he says. 

“But you’ll find in the background a couple of guys working in the supply chain screaming ‘Please, don’t do this to us again, because every ten years you do the same thing, and in five years’ time you’ll come back and say ‘Where’s the whisky? I’ve got massive growing demand’.” 

Whisky producers cutting back

Time will tell, but it’s fair to say that Diageo is not the only Scotch producer cutting back. The independent whisky firm of Ian Macleod Distillers lowered production at its Glengoyne and Rosebank distilleries by 30 per cent this year, while there have intermittent pauses at LVMH’s Glenmorangie distillery and at Brown Forman’s Glenglassaugh and Benriach distilleries.

Brown Forman, famous for Jack Daniel’s, is well aware of the oversupply of American whiskey. The state of Kentucky is drowning in bourbon with 16.2m barrels in its warehouses at the start of the year, compared to less than 6m a decade ago. 

Much of the reason for these vast stocks can be put down to speculation. Prospectors were lured in by the promise of quick returns. It was said you could fill a barrel for $750 and flog it for $4,000 four years later to someone who would bottle it up and sell it on. There was no brand or market in sight from the outset, and in the end, there were no buyers either.

There was a similar if somewhat smaller, whiskey ‘Gold Rush’ in Ireland where the speculators have since vanished, leaving the banks who financed the stock licking their wounds. As in America, the big brands will survive, though there are plenty of deals to help drain supply. Jameson’s is on semi-permanent discount in Irish supermarkets, apparently.

Irish and American whiskey share a similar business model for new entrants to the category whereby you conceive your brand, cook up some alluring backstory, buy the liquid from a contract distiller, and tell everyone your dream is to open your own distillery one day.

It all helped to inflate a big speculative bubble that has since burst. In the UK, there was a similar stampede into gin with an explosion of new brands that came and went. But with Scotch whisky, this didn’t happen because there isn’t that model of contract distilling. 

“We’ve obviously got the secondary market, and there are independent bottlers and cask investment companies, but it’s small,” says Rupert Patrick, founder & CEO of indy bottler James Eadie. “Relative to the total size of the market, it’s not even 1 per cent.”

Having worked for Diageo among other big players, he sympathises with those like Ewan Andrew tasked with trying to forecast demand in these turbulent times. “It is a massive game of chess for them,” he says. Getting predictions long or short is par for the course. “At the moment most people are probably slightly long, but maybe by 3 – 4 per cent. I don’t think by much more.”

Scotch also has various tricks up its sleeve to help manage its inventory of maturing stocks. “We’ve gone through age statements, no age statements, over-ageing, under-ageing, all sorts of things,” says Rupert. “The industry is very good at adapting to the scenario.”

Aldi took on more than £100m in net debt last year, as the discount grocer’s profit slipped despite its blockbuster expansion plans.  The supermarket chain, the UK’s fourth largest, saw its net debt grow by a fifth in 2025, from £717m to £862m.  Aldi’s jump in debt comes despite the grocer’s plans to expand rapidly [...]]]>

Aldi took on more than £100m in net debt last year, as the discount grocer’s profit slipped despite its blockbuster expansion plans. 

The supermarket chain, the UK’s fourth largest, saw its net debt grow by a fifth in 2025, from £717m to £862m. 

Aldi’s jump in debt comes despite the grocer’s plans to expand rapidly in the UK. Last week, chief executive Giles Hurley announced £900m in funding to open 40 new stores next year.

Hurley said last week that the supermarket’s operating profit held steady at £433m last year, though new company filings show its pre-tax profit slipped from £416m to £400m.

The family-owned grocer’s workforce fell from 50,655 to 49,661 in the year to December 2025, its filings revealed, suggesting it cut about 1,000 staff in the year. 

Despite the falling headcount, the supermarket chain’s wage costs jumped from £1.43bn to £1.46bn.

Aldi eyes more market share

Aldi’s increase in debt comes from borrowing from its parent company, rather than external lending from banks, it is understood. The grocer’s debt pile, while rising, remains well below that of some of its private-equity-owned rivals. 

Net debt at Morrisons, which is owned by New York-based Clayton, Dubilier & Rice, jumped from £7.1bn to £7.5bn in the year to October. Asda, owned by London-based TDR Capital, has debts of £3.5bn. 

While Asda and Morrisons have sought to sell off the freehold rights to some of its shops in a bid to push down their debt piles, Aldi is hoping to put more pressure on the UK’s ‘big four’ supermarkets. 

Aldi and fellow German discounter Lidl have surged to dominance of Britain’s grocery market in recent decades. Morrisons is now the UK’s fifth-biggest supermarket, having been leapfrogged by Aldi in 2022.

Aldi is within one per cent of Asda’s market share, though its control of the market has weakened from 10.8 to 10.6 per cent over the past year, according to figures from Worldpanel. 

Announcing the grocer’s results last week, Hurley hit out at rival supermarkets for offering loyalty discounts, which he says give shoppers a misleading impression of value.

He told reporters: “One of the drivers of their growth is the fact that their retail prices are going up, and some of them are seeing volume decline at the same time.

“We are driving prices down, and we’re growing our volumes, and that is hugely important in continuing to reinforce our confidence around growing our business and expanding.”

Aldi UK is part of the grocery chain’s Aldi Sud branch, which is controlled by the heirs of Karl Albrecht. He co-founded the grocer with his brother, Theo, in 1946.

Aldi was contacted for comment.

IG’s shares plunged in early morning trading on Friday after it was forced to cut its annual revenue forecast.

The spread betting company saw its share drop 26 per cent to 950p per share. Shares are down 23.7 per cent since January.

The sharp fall follows the group’s revenue falling 14 per cent year on year during the third quarter after it retained less of its customer’s trading activity as revenue on over the counter trading (OTC) business.

OTC trading is where customers can trade assets without using a primary stock exchange.

OTC revenue retention slid to 70 per cent from 80 per cent, which the FTSE 100 group has averaged since its introduction in the second half of 2025.

The online trading platform now expects full year revenue growth to be in “a mid-single-digit per cent range” year on year.

The platform had previously expected revenue to increase between 10 and 15 per cent on an organic basis, after hiking its performance outlook in May.

Market conditions

Earnings before tax are anticipated to be in the “low-40s per cent range” for the financial year, a decline from last period’s 47 per cent.

Chief executive Breon Corcoran blamed the decline on “less supportive market conditions”, as despite the fall in revenue customer demand remained robust.

Organic first trades rose more than 25 per cent, while active customer numbers climbed 17 per cent.

Income generated from OTC customers also grew eight per cent.

The investing platform’s acquisition Underdog, a sports prediction market, also saw net revenue more than double to $105m, ahead of its “seasonally important” fourth quarter.

But the Board expects to meet its medium-term guidance beyond 2026, anticipating further customer growth off the back of continued investment into products coupled with “higher OTC revenue retention.

Energy secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh is holding crunch talks with her American counterpart about an escalating diesel spat that has seen Treasury secretary Scott Bessent urge Europe to release emergency reserves “immediately”.

City AM understands that Fahnbulleh is in direct contact with US energy secretary Chris Wright to discuss a US move to potentially choke off diesel exports to Europe that threatens to upend supply and send prices at the pump soaring, a person familiar with the discussions said.

The UK and Europe are being pressured by the Trump administration to tap into their emergency stockpiles of the fuel to relieve a major global shortage sparked by the conflict in the Middle East.

The President is weighing a range of protectionist trade measures should Europe refuse to release its reserves, ranging from curbing exports to select countries to an all out ban on US-produced diesel.

On Wednesday, Bessent ramped up pressure on European allies, telling them to tap into their stockpiles “immediately” and “match… their commitments with action”. In a post on social media, he wrote: “Our European partners should accelerate delivery on their existing commitments and make additional supplies immediately available to address ongoing disruptions.”

He added that American truck drivers, farmers and businesses “should not be left carrying the burden of a global diesel fuel shortage”.

Europe has been racing to agree a joint response to the US’s pressure, which comes just weeks before the country’s pivotal mid-term elections in which prices at the pump have become a major talking point.

Energy minister Martin McCluskey joined a call with EU commissioners on Thursday to weigh their response, a person familliar with discussions said. But participants could not commit any concrete actions beyond agreeing “to maintain close contact” as events develop.

America’s broadsides are believed to be aimed predominantly at France and Germany, which have access to a considerably larger pool of emergency reserves than the UK.

Diesel prices ‘extreme’ – Healey

But any loss of US diesel would be enormously damaging for Britain, which currently imports over half its supply of the refined fuel. Roughly a third of that currently comes from the States, meaning any ban would choke off one of the country’s major sources of supply in an already starved global market.

Adding to the situation’s severity is the prospect of Britain’s largest refinery shuttering its operations for 10 weeks as for planned maintenance. The Fawley site in Hampshire is responsible for producing kerosene for Heathrow and a fifth of diesel used at British forecourts.

Diesel prices have been rising across the globe, as some of the world’s largest refineries became targets in both the Middle East and Ukraine conflicts. In Britain, the fuel has climbed to 200p a litre, nearing the record set during the height of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

For drivers, the rise means it costs almost £110 to fill up a typical family car, £31 more than before the onset of the Iran war.

Chancellor John Healey acknowledged diesel prices were “extreme” in an interview at Labour party conference.

“In the end, we’re also working with the Americans where we can try and put in place what will solve this, or at least significantly ease it,” he said, “which would be a diplomatic settlement [and] an end to the fighting with Iran.”

A spoksewoman for the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero said: “We have a diverse and resilient supply. We continue to engage with our international partners and the UK fuel industry.”

Pub chain Wetherspoon has hit out at the government for causing “high street dereliction” by hiking taxes, as the company’s profit slipped by a quarter. 

The London-listed pub group saw revenue jump by five per cent to £2.2bn in the year to July – in line with analyst forecasts – though pre-tax profit fell further than expected, by 28 per cent to £59m. 

Sir Tim Martin, Wetherspoon’s chairman, blamed the Labour government for hiking business rates, minimum wages and national insurance contributions (NICs). 

He said: “The hospitality industry, as many commentators and companies have noted, has borne the brunt of government-led tax and regulatory cost increases, especially in the last two budgets. 

“This has resulted in pubs becoming even more expensive than supermarkets, leading to job losses, closures and high street dereliction.”

Wetherspoon is famed for its rock-bottom prices, but analysts have predicted that this could mean rising taxes and energy costs will weigh more heavily on it than some of its higher-margin rivals.  The pubco’s operating margin slimmed from 6.9 to 5.4 per cent in the last year. 

Heatwaves boost summer sales

The FTSE 250 pub firm blamed a five per cent increase in costs for its falling profit. The group paid £46 more in wages, £31m more in repairs and £9m more in business rates last year.

Wetherspoon’s energy costs jumped by 77 per cent to £40m last year, it told shareholders. Energy costs and packaging taxes have also “weighed heavily” on hospitality firms in recent years, Martin said. 

The pub firm said its sales picked up in recent months, helped by “exceptional weather”. Like-for-like sales grew by 8.6 per cent in the last nine weeks, it said. 

This has been helped by “substantial progress in recent years in increasing the number of beer gardens and outside seating areas”. 

Martin claimed Wetherspoon is outperforming the wider pub sector. Like-for-like sales at the company grew by 7.7 per cent in August, compared to sector-wide growth of 0.8 per cent, according to NIQ figures. 

The pub boss told City AM that his attempts to keep prices low may be to blame for the firm’s drop in profit. He said: “I think everyone knows that Wetherspoon has a restrained attitude to pricing, which you could argue can cause short-term underperformance.”

Martin did not rule out hiking prices to keep up with rising costs. He said: “It was 48p per pint when I started. We have put our prices up, but we just haven’t put them up as much as everyone else. We’ve no plans to change our general approach as of today.”

The Wetherspoon boss reiterated his calls for John Healey to cut VAT on hospitality firms from 20 to 10 per cent. 

The pub chain has backed a campaign, led by celebrity chef Tom Kerridge, which claims this tax break would be the easiest way to prevent swathes of insolvencies and job losses on the high street.

Shares in JD Wetherspoon jumped eight per cent to 880.5p in early trading.
